# Speaker Platform Without Fees: Get Booked and Keep 100% of Your Fee

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/speaker-platform-without-fees/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**A speaker platform without fees lets you list your talks, get found by event planners and receive booking requests without paying a membership, a listing fee or a commission on what you earn.** Most options charge in one of those three ways: speakers bureaus usually take 25% to 30% of your fee, and many speaker marketplaces charge a monthly subscription. Speakerfolio is free for speakers: you get a speaker website and a profile in the speaker directory, planners contact you directly, and you keep 100% of your fee.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **"Free" can hide fees.** Check for subscriptions, paid upgrades to appear in search, lead fees and booking commissions.
> - **Bureaus earn by commission**, usually 25% to 30% of the speaker's fee. That's fair when they bring you work you couldn't get yourself.
> - **Paid marketplaces charge monthly** whether or not you get booked.
> - **A no-fee platform plus your own website** gives you visibility now and keeps every booking yours.

## What "without fees" should actually mean

When you compare speaker platforms, look past the word "free" on the sign-up page. A platform is only free for speakers if all of these are true:

- **No membership or subscription** to keep your profile live
- **No listing fee** to appear in search results or the directory
- **No commission** taken from the fees you agree with clients
- **No charge per lead** or per booking request
- **Direct contact** with event planners, so the platform doesn't sit in the middle of the deal

If a platform is free to join but charges to show your video, unlock leads or appear above other speakers, it's a free trial of a paid product.

## How speaker platforms charge: the four common models

| Model | How you pay | What it typically costs | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speakers bureau | Commission on each booking | Usually 25% to 30% of your fee | Established speakers with high fees |
| Paid speaker marketplace | Monthly or yearly subscription | For example, SpeakerMatch plans run $30 to $80 every 4 weeks | Speakers who want paid lead lists |
| Freemium profile site | Free basic profile, paid upgrades | Extra features such as more videos sit behind paid tiers | Speakers testing the waters |
| No-fee platform (Speakerfolio) | Nothing | $0, with no commission on bookings | New and growing speakers who want to keep every booking |

None of these models is wrong. A bureau that books you at $15,000 has earned its share. The problem is paying fees before you have the bookings to cover them.

## Why speakers look for a platform without fees

### Your margin stays yours

On a $5,000 keynote, a 25% commission is $1,250. Over ten bookings a year, that's $12,500. If the platform didn't find the client, you shouldn't have to pay for the introduction.

### Subscriptions cost money even in quiet months

A monthly plan keeps charging whether you speak twice that month or not at all. For new speakers with uneven bookings, those costs add up before the first paid talk.

### Planners like talking to you directly

Event planners want quick answers about your topic, availability and fee. When requests come straight to your inbox, you can reply the same day, tailor your talk and build a relationship that leads to repeat bookings.

## Hidden fees to check before you sign up

Read the pricing page and the terms. Look for:

1. **Upgrade walls**: your profile is free, but video, photos or contact details need a paid plan.
2. **Pay-to-rank**: paid members appear first, so free profiles sit on page five.
3. **Lead or pitch fees**: you pay to see or apply for speaking opportunities.
4. **Booking commission**: a percentage of the fee when a booking comes through the platform.
5. **Payment processing**: the platform collects the fee from the client and keeps a cut before paying you.
6. **Lock-in**: your profile, reviews or contacts disappear if you stop paying.

## What a good no-fee speaker platform includes

Free shouldn't mean bare. Look for:

| Feature | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| A full profile with talks and topics | Planners shortlist by topic and format |
| Stage video | The first thing most planners want to see |
| Testimonials and past events | Proof that lowers the planner's risk |
| A booking request form | Gets you the event date, audience and budget up front |
| Your own speaker website | Somewhere to send people that isn't just a profile on someone else's site |
| Search visibility | So planners find you on Google and through AI assistants |

## Speakerfolio: a speaker platform with no fees

Speakerfolio is a speaker directory where every speaker has a real website. It's a [speaker platform without fees](https://speakerfolio.com/), built so speakers can get found and booked without paying for the privilege.

Here's what you get for free:

## How to get listed on a no-fee speaker platform

### Step 1: Prepare your basics

Have your LinkedIn profile up to date, a clear headshot and a link to at least one talk on YouTube or Vimeo. Even a phone recording of a recent talk is better than nothing.

"Leading Through Change: Keep Your Best People When Everything Shifts" tells a planner more than "Leadership". Add three takeaways for each talk.

## When paying for a platform or bureau makes sense

A no-fee platform isn't the only tool you'll ever need. Paying can be worth it when:

- A bureau has relationships with corporate buyers in your field and books you at higher fees
- You need a large, curated database of speaking opportunities to pitch
- You want a full agency to handle contracts, travel and invoicing

Many speakers use both: a free platform and website for direct bookings, and a bureau for larger engagements. Just make sure you're not paying commission on clients who found you themselves.

# How Organizations Select Business Keynote Speakers: The 7-Stage Process

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-organizations-select-business-keynote-speakers/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**Organizations select business keynote speakers by matching a speaker's topic and style to the event's goal, then checking proof: stage video, testimonials from similar companies, and a short call to test fit.** The decision usually involves an event lead, an executive sponsor and often HR, marketing or procurement, and it moves through stages from a brief to a shortlist to a contract. Speakers who make that process easy get chosen more often. Planners can compare business speakers side by side in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/).

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **The event goal comes first.** Companies pick the speaker who best serves the outcome they need, not the most famous name.
> - **Several people decide.** An event lead shortlists, an executive approves, and procurement or legal often signs off.
> - **Proof wins:** stage video, testimonials from similar companies, and clear talk outcomes.
> - **Speakers who are easy to evaluate** (clear website, fast replies, simple pricing) move to the top of the shortlist.

## Who decides which business keynote speaker gets booked

At most companies, choosing a keynote speaker isn't one person's call. These are the people usually involved:

| Role | What they care about |
|---|---|
| Event manager or planner | Fit with the agenda, logistics, reliability, budget |
| Executive sponsor (CEO, CHRO, sales leader) | Whether the message supports the company's strategy |
| HR or learning and development | Whether employees will learn and apply something |
| Marketing or communications | Brand fit, tone and how the talk will look on social media |
| Procurement or legal | Contract terms, insurance, invoicing and approved suppliers |
| Event agency or speakers bureau (if used) | Finding options that meet the brief and budget |

A speaker might impress the event manager and still lose because the executive sponsor wants a different message. The best speakers make it easy for the event lead to "sell" them internally.

## The 7-stage selection process

### Stage 1: Define the event goal

It starts with a question: what should change because of this event? Typical answers for business events:

- Align teams behind a new strategy
- Energise a sales force before a big year
- Help leaders through a merger, restructure or new technology
- Build culture and connection after a hard year
- Position the company as a thought leader at a client or industry event

The goal shapes everything else, from topic to tone to budget.

### Stage 2: Write the speaker brief

The event lead writes a short brief, often one page, covering:

- Audience: who, how many, seniority and industry
- Theme and goal of the event
- Format: opening keynote, closing keynote, fireside chat, virtual
- Length, date and location
- Budget range
- Must-haves, such as industry experience or a specific topic

### Stage 3: Build a longlist

Next, the team gathers 10 to 20 possible names. Business event planners usually find them through:

- Speaker directories, where they can filter by topic and format
- Speakers bureaus and event agencies
- Recommendations from colleagues and other companies
- Speakers they've seen at conferences
- Google, LinkedIn and AI assistants
- Authors of books the leadership team admires

At this stage, the speaker's online presence matters most. If the planner can't quickly see the topic, a video and a way to book, the speaker often doesn't make the next cut.

### Stage 4: Shortlist with clear criteria

The team narrows the list to three to five speakers using criteria like these:

| Criteria | What planners look for |
|---|---|
| Topic fit | A talk that matches the event goal, not a generic one |
| Business credibility | Real experience in leadership, sales, operations or the industry |
| Stage presence | Video of the speaker holding a large room |
| Relevant clients | Past talks for similar companies, sizes or industries |
| Tailoring | Willingness to adapt examples and language to the company |
| Takeaways | Practical ideas the audience can use the next day |
| Budget | Fee, travel and extras within the approved range |
| Availability | Free on the date, including travel time |

Many teams score each speaker from 1 to 5 on these points to compare them fairly and explain the choice to leadership.

### Stage 5: Check proof and references

For the shortlist, planners dig deeper:

- Watch full talks, not only a highlight reel
- Read testimonials and look for names and companies they recognise
- Call or message a past client for a reference
- Look at recent articles, podcasts or books
- Check the speaker's social media for tone and anything off-brand

### Stage 6: Hold a fit call

Before deciding, many organizations have a 20 to 30 minute call with their top one or two speakers. They're testing:

- How well the speaker listens and asks about the audience
- How they'd tailor the talk to the company's situation
- Whether their energy and values fit the culture
- How easy they'll be to work with on logistics

A speaker who arrives with good questions and a few ideas for tailoring often wins at this stage.

### Stage 7: Approve, contract and prepare

Once the team agrees, the executive sponsor approves the choice and procurement handles the contract. The agreement usually covers the fee and deposit, travel, recording rights, cancellation terms and any extra sessions. Then comes a prep call to plan the details.

## What business organizations value most in a keynote speaker

When companies explain why they picked one speaker over another, the reasons tend to be the same:

1. **The talk fit our goal.** The message clearly supported what leadership wanted to achieve.
2. **They understood business.** The speaker had credibility with managers and executives, not only inspiration.
3. **We could see them in action.** Strong video removed the risk.
4. **Others like us trusted them.** Testimonials from similar companies made the decision easier to defend.
5. **They were easy to work with.** Fast, clear replies and simple terms.

## Red flags that get speakers dropped

- A website or profile that hasn't been updated in years
- No full-length video, only short clips
- Generic talks that can't be tailored
- Slow replies or unclear pricing
- Testimonials with no names or companies
- Content online that clashes with the company's values
- Pushing to sell products or coaching during the keynote

## How business keynote speakers can get selected more often

If you're a speaker, use the selection process to your advantage:

- **Lead with outcomes:** describe each talk by what changes for the audience, not just the topic.
- **Show business proof:** client logos, case studies and testimonials from managers and executives.
- **Make video easy to find:** a short reel and at least one full talk.
- **Publish a clear booking path:** formats, rough fee range and a simple enquiry form.
- **Reply fast and ask smart questions:** it signals how easy you'll be to work with.
- **Be findable:** a speaker website and directory profile so you appear when planners search.

## How Speakerfolio helps organizations and speakers

**For organizations**, the Speakerfolio speaker directory lists business speakers with their topics, talks, formats and booking details in one consistent layout, so your team can build a longlist and compare speakers quickly. Browsing and contacting speakers is free. For a step-by-step planning guide, see how to [find a keynote speaker](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-find-a-keynote-speaker/), and for budgets, our guide to [keynote speakers for hire](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/keynote-speakers-for-hire/).

**For business keynote speakers**, Speakerfolio writes and builds a free speaker website from your LinkedIn profile, with your talks, video, client proof and a booking form, on yourname.speakerfolio.com, and lists you in the directory. Premium moves your site to your own domain with a custom design and full control for $100 a year, hosting and updates included.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do companies choose a keynote speaker?

They start with the event goal and audience, write a brief, build a longlist from directories, bureaus and referrals, shortlist three to five speakers against clear criteria, check video and references, hold a fit call and then contract the best match.

### Who decides on the keynote speaker for a corporate event?

Usually the event manager shortlists, an executive sponsor approves, and HR, marketing, procurement or legal may also be involved depending on the company.

### What do organizations look for in a business keynote speaker?

Topic fit with the event goal, business credibility, stage presence on video, experience with similar companies, willingness to tailor the talk, practical takeaways, budget fit and availability.

### How far in advance do companies book keynote speakers?

Most book three to nine months ahead. Large conferences and high-demand speakers are often booked nine to twelve months in advance.

### How much do businesses pay for keynote speakers?

Fees range widely: emerging speakers often charge $1,500 to $5,000, established professionals $5,000 to $30,000, and celebrities $30,000 or more, plus travel.

### Why do companies hold a call before booking a speaker?

To check how the speaker listens, how they'd tailor the talk, whether they fit the culture and how easy they'll be to work with.

### How can a speaker get chosen by more organizations?

Describe talks by their outcomes, show business proof and video, make booking simple, reply quickly and have a speaker website and directory profile so planners can find and evaluate you.

## Make the right choice, or be the right choice

Organizations choose business keynote speakers the same way they make other important decisions: clear goals, clear criteria and proof. Planners can start building a shortlist in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/). Speakers can get their [free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start) built and listed, so they're easy to evaluate when the brief arrives.

# How to Become a Community Speaker: 8 Steps to Speaking Where You Live

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-become-a-community-speaker/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**To become a community speaker, pick a cause or topic your community cares about, prepare one clear talk on it, and start speaking at local groups such as libraries, schools, nonprofits, service clubs and neighbourhood associations.** Say yes to panels and small events, build relationships with local organisers, and collect testimonials and video as you go. When people start asking how to book you, a speaker website and a profile in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/) make it easy for them to find you.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Community speakers are known locally** for a cause, skill or experience, not for fame.
> - **Start with the groups you already belong to**, then widen to libraries, schools, clubs and nonprofits.
> - **Have two formats ready:** a 20 to 30 minute talk and a shorter version for panels and events.
> - **Relationships drive bookings.** One good talk often leads to three more invitations.

## What is a community speaker?

A community speaker gives talks to local audiences about issues, skills or experiences that matter to the people around them. They speak at town halls, libraries, schools, places of worship, nonprofit events, business groups, festivals and panel discussions.

Community speakers are often:

- Nonprofit leaders and volunteers sharing a cause
- Health, safety or education professionals giving practical advice
- Local business owners talking about entrepreneurship
- People with lived experience, such as recovery, immigration, caregiving or overcoming hardship
- Youth workers, coaches and mentors
- Faith leaders speaking beyond their own congregation
- Activists and organisers working on local issues

## Community speaker vs other speakers

| | Community speaker | Keynote speaker | Motivational speaker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main audience | Local groups and organisations | Conferences and companies | Schools, teams, companies |
| Typical setting | Libraries, clubs, nonprofits, panels | Large events and conferences | Assemblies, kick-offs, events |
| Main goal | Inform, connect and mobilise locally | Set the theme of an event | Inspire people to act |
| Typical fee | Often free to modest honorarium | Paid, often by experience | Paid, often by experience |

Many speakers do all three over time. Community speaking is often where they start. If inspiring people is your main goal, our guide on how to become a [motivational speaker](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-become-a-motivational-speaker/) covers that path.

## How to become a community speaker: 8 steps

### Step 1: Choose your cause or topic

Start with what you know and care about. Ask yourself:

- What do people in my community come to me for advice about?
- What problem in my area am I trying to solve?
- What have I lived through that could help others?

Good community topics are specific and local: "How families in our county can access free mental health support" connects better than "mental health".

### Step 2: Know who needs to hear it

Picture the people in the room. Are they parents, small business owners, seniors, teenagers, new residents, volunteers? Each group needs different examples and a different call to action. Write down two or three audiences and the groups they belong to.

### Step 3: Prepare one talk and a short version

Build a core talk of 20 to 30 minutes with a simple shape:

1. **A local story** that shows why the issue matters here
2. **The problem** and who it affects
3. **What's working**, including your own work or organisation
4. **What the audience can do**, with one clear next step

Then cut a five-minute version you can use on panels, at events and when an organiser gives you "a few minutes at the start".

### Step 4: Start with groups you already belong to

Your first audiences are often closer than you think: your workplace, your place of worship, your children's school, your gym, your volunteer group. Offer to speak at a meeting or lunch. These friendly rooms are where you'll practise and get your first testimonials.

### Step 5: Find local stages

Once you've given a few talks, reach out further. Common places that book community speakers:

| Where | What they often want |
|---|---|
| Public libraries | Free workshops and talks for residents |
| Schools and colleges | Career talks, assemblies, parent evenings |
| Rotary, Lions and service clubs | 20 to 30 minute lunch or breakfast talks |
| Chambers of commerce | Business, leadership and local economy topics |
| Nonprofits and charities | Fundraisers, volunteer events, awareness days |
| Places of worship | Community issues, family, outreach |
| Neighbourhood associations | Safety, local services, civic issues |
| Local festivals and fairs | Panels, short talks and demos |
| Local podcasts and radio | Interviews on community topics |

Find the programme chair or events coordinator, and send a short email with your topic, who it helps and a link to your website or speaker profile.

### Step 6: Say yes to panels and Q&As

Panels are one of the easiest ways into community speaking. You share the stage, the pressure is lower and organisers often need more voices. Prepare two or three short points you want to make and a story you can tell in under a minute. If nerves hold you back, our guide on building [confidence in public speaking](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-build-confidence-in-public-speaking/) can help.

### Step 7: Build relationships, not just bookings

Community speaking runs on trust and word of mouth. After each event:

- Thank the organiser in writing
- Ask for a short testimonial
- Ask who else they know who might want the talk
- Stay in touch with useful updates, not just requests
- Show up to other community events, even when you're not speaking

One talk at a Rotary club can lead to invitations from members' businesses, schools and charities.

### Step 8: Make yourself easy to find

As word spreads, people will search for you. Organisers want to see what you speak about, a short video and how to reach you. A simple speaker website brings it together: your topics, your story, testimonials, upcoming events and a contact form. It also helps people find you on Google and through AI assistants when they search for local speakers on your topic.

## Do community speakers get paid?

Sometimes. Many community talks are free or come with a small honorarium, especially for nonprofits, libraries and schools. As you build a reputation, you can:

- Ask for an honorarium from organisations with event budgets
- Charge businesses and conferences a speaking fee
- Seek sponsorship from local businesses for a talk series
- Apply for community or arts grants that fund public programmes
- Offer paid workshops alongside free talks

Being clear about what you charge and when you speak for free makes it easier for organisers to say yes.

## Mistakes new community speakers make

- Choosing a topic so broad that it doesn't feel local
- Talking about the problem without giving the audience something to do
- Only speaking where they're already known
- Not asking for testimonials or referrals after a talk
- Turning up without a short version when the schedule runs late
- Having no website or profile, so organisers can't share their details

## How Speakerfolio helps community speakers

Speakerfolio builds websites for speakers, trainers and coaches. You send your LinkedIn profile, and we write and build a free one-page speaker website for you, with your story, topics, testimonials, upcoming events and a contact form, on yourname.speakerfolio.com.

You're also listed in the Speakerfolio speaker directory, where organisers search for speakers by topic. Our Spotlight template is designed for faith and community speakers, with sections for messages, upcoming gatherings and invite options. When you want your own domain and a custom design, Premium is $100 a year with hosting and updates included.

## Frequently asked questions

### What does a community speaker do?

A community speaker gives talks to local audiences about issues, skills or experiences that matter to them, at places like libraries, schools, nonprofits, service clubs, places of worship and community events.

### How do I start speaking in my community?

Choose one topic you know well, prepare a 20 to 30 minute talk and a short version, and offer to speak at groups you already belong to. Then contact libraries, schools, service clubs and nonprofits in your area.

### Do I need experience to become a community speaker?

No. Many community speakers start with lived experience or local knowledge rather than speaking experience. Friendly local groups are a good place to practise.

### Where can I find community speaking opportunities?

Public libraries, schools, Rotary and Lions clubs, chambers of commerce, nonprofits, places of worship, neighbourhood associations, local festivals and local podcasts all invite community speakers.

### Do community speakers get paid?

Many community talks are free or include a small honorarium. Speakers often charge businesses and conferences, use sponsorships or grants for talk series, and offer paid workshops.

### How do I contact organisations to speak?

Find the programme chair or events coordinator and send a short email with your topic, who it helps, the format and length, and a link to your website or speaker profile.

### How do I become a better community speaker?

Speak often, record your talks, ask for feedback, and adapt each talk to the specific audience. Keep stories local and always give people a clear next step.

## Start speaking where you live

Becoming a community speaker starts with one topic you care about and one room that needs to hear it. Speak to the groups you know, build relationships with local organisers and make it easy for them to find you. Get your [free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start) from Speakerfolio and join the speaker directory.

# How to Become a Motivational Speaker: 9 Steps From Story to Stage

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-become-a-motivational-speaker/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**To become a motivational speaker, start with a real story of change you've lived, turn it into one clear message, and choose the audience that most needs to hear it.** Build a signature talk around that message, practise it at schools, community groups and company events, and collect video and testimonials as you go. Then make yourself easy to book with a speaker website and a profile in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/), where event planners search for speakers.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Your story is the foundation**, but the talk has to be about the audience's change, not only yours.
> - **Pick a niche:** students, sales teams, athletes, nonprofits or faith groups all need different talks.
> - **Start small and speak often.** Video and testimonials from early talks are what get you bigger bookings.
> - **Motivational speakers earn from more than keynotes**: workshops, coaching, books and online programmes add income.

## What does a motivational speaker do?

A motivational speaker gives talks that help people see what's possible and take action. Their talks usually mix a personal story with practical lessons, and they're booked to lift energy, change mindsets or rally a group behind a goal.

Motivational speakers speak at:

- Company kick-offs, sales conferences and team offsites
- Schools, colleges and graduation events
- Nonprofit galas and fundraisers
- Sports teams and athletic programmes
- Churches and faith-based events
- Community events and youth programmes

Many motivational speakers are booked as the keynote speaker at an event. If you want to understand the keynote role more broadly, our guide on [what a keynote speaker does](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-does-a-keynote-speaker-do/) explains it.

## What makes a great motivational speaker

The best motivational speakers share a few things:

| Quality | What it looks like on stage |
|---|---|
| A real story | They've lived what they talk about, so the audience trusts them |
| A clear message | The audience can repeat the main idea after the talk |
| Practical takeaways | People leave with something to do, not just a good feeling |
| Energy that fits the room | They can lift a tired room or speak quietly to a small one |
| Humility | The story serves the audience; the speaker isn't the hero of every moment |

## How to become a motivational speaker: 9 steps

### Step 1: Find your story

Every motivational talk starts with a story of change. It might be overcoming an illness, rebuilding after failure, leaving a career, leading a team through a crisis, growing up with very little or achieving something people said you couldn't.

Write down the key moments: where you started, what went wrong, the turning point, what you did and where you are now. You don't need a dramatic story. You need an honest one that others can see themselves in.

### Step 2: Turn your story into a message

A story alone isn't a talk. Ask: what did this teach me that would help someone else? That lesson is your message.

Try finishing this sentence: "After my talk, people will believe they can... because..." For example: "After my talk, young people will believe they can recover from a bad start, because I'll show them the three choices that changed my life."

### Step 3: Choose your audience

Motivational speaking is a crowded field, and a clear niche helps planners choose you. Pick one main audience to start with:

| Audience | What they often need |
|---|---|
| Students and young people | Belief, direction, resilience, avoiding risky choices |
| Sales teams | Drive, handling rejection, hitting targets |
| Corporate teams | Resilience, change, teamwork, wellbeing |
| Athletes and sports teams | Mental toughness, focus, comeback stories |
| Nonprofits and fundraisers | Purpose, hope, inspiring donors and volunteers |
| Faith communities | Purpose, healing, service, family |

You can speak to other audiences later, but one clear focus makes your marketing much easier.

### Step 4: Build a signature talk

Your signature talk is the one you'll give again and again, adapted for each audience. A simple structure works for most motivational talks:

1. **Opening moment:** drop the audience into a key scene from your story
2. **The struggle:** what was at stake and why it was hard
3. **The turning point:** the moment or choice that changed things
4. **The lessons:** three practical ideas the audience can apply
5. **The call to action:** what you want them to do next

Keep the focus on the audience. A good test: for every story about you, there should be a clear "and here's what that means for you."

### Step 5: Practise on smaller stages

Start where the stakes are low and the audience is real:

- Local schools and youth groups
- Rotary clubs, chambers of commerce and community groups
- Churches and faith groups
- Your own workplace or industry association
- Online events, webinars and podcasts
- Toastmasters or another speaking club

Speak for free at first if it gets you in front of the right people. Ask every organiser if you can record the talk.

### Step 6: Record your talks and collect testimonials

Planners want to see you speak before they book you. Record every talk you can, even on a phone, and cut your best moments into a two-minute [speaker reel](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/make-a-two-minute-speaker-reel-from-footage-you-already-have/).

After each event, ask the organiser for a short testimonial with their name, role and organisation. Quotes about what changed for the audience are the most convincing.

### Step 7: Create your speaker materials

Before you start pitching, have these ready:

- A short and a long speaker bio
- Professional photos, including one of you on stage
- Your signature talk title and description
- Your speaker reel
- Testimonials
- A one-page speaker sheet with all of the above

### Step 8: Get a motivational speaker website

When planners hear your name, they look you up. They also ask AI assistants for motivational speakers on topics like resilience or leadership. Without a website, they have very little to judge you by.

Your website should show your story, your talks, your reel, testimonials, the audiences you speak to and a booking form. Our checklist on what a [motivational speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/motivational-speaker-website-checklist/) needs covers each section.

### Step 9: Start pitching and set your fees

With your talk, video, testimonials and website ready, start contacting events in your niche. Find the person who books speakers, send a short message about why your talk fits their audience and include a link to your website.

As your experience grows, set your fees:

| Speaker level | Typical fee per talk |
|---|---|
| New speaker | Free to $1,500 |
| Emerging speaker | $1,500 to $5,000 |
| Established speaker | $5,000 to $30,000 |
| Well-known name or bestselling author | $30,000+ |

Many motivational speakers charge less for schools and nonprofits and more for corporate events.

## How motivational speakers make money

Speaking fees are only one part. Many motivational speakers also earn from:

- **Workshops and training** that go deeper than a keynote
- **Coaching** for individuals or small groups
- **Books**, often sold at events
- **Online courses and programmes**
- **Virtual talks** for remote teams and online events
- **Sponsorships and partnerships** with brands that share their message

Offering more than one format also makes it easier for organisers to book you, especially when budgets are tight.

## Common mistakes new motivational speakers make

- Telling their story without turning it into lessons for the audience
- Trying to speak to everyone instead of choosing a niche
- Relying on emotion alone, with no practical takeaways
- Not recording talks, so there's no video when planners ask
- Waiting until everything is perfect before speaking anywhere
- Having only a social media page instead of a proper website

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I become a motivational speaker with no experience?

Start with your own story of change, turn it into one clear message and practise at schools, community groups, clubs and online events. Record your talks, collect testimonials and build a speaker website so organisers can find and book you.

### Do you need a degree to be a motivational speaker?

No. Motivational speakers are booked for their story, message and ability to connect with an audience, not for a specific qualification.

### How much do motivational speakers make?

New motivational speakers often start free or under $1,500 per talk. Emerging speakers usually charge $1,500 to $5,000, and established speakers $5,000 to $30,000 or more. Many also earn from workshops, coaching and books.

### What should a motivational speech include?

A personal story, a clear message, practical lessons the audience can use and a call to action. The audience should leave knowing what to do next, not just feeling inspired.

### How do motivational speakers get booked?

Through speaker websites, speaker directories, referrals from past organisers, speakers bureaus and direct outreach to events in their niche. Video and testimonials are usually what convince a planner to book.

### What is the difference between a motivational speaker and a keynote speaker?

A motivational speaker is defined by the style and goal of their talks: inspiring people to act. A keynote speaker is defined by their role at an event: giving the main talk. Many motivational speakers are booked as keynote speakers.

### How long does it take to become a motivational speaker?

It depends on how often you speak and how clear your niche is. Many speakers get their first paid booking after a series of free or low-fee talks that give them video, testimonials and referrals.

# How to Improve Public Speaking: 11 Skills to Practise

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-improve-public-speaking/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**To improve public speaking, work on one skill at a time: a clear structure, a steady voice, open body language, and stories that make your points stick.** Record your practice runs, watch them back and ask for honest feedback after every talk. Then speak as often as you can, from team meetings to small events, because skill grows with repetition. Once your talks are strong, a speaker website and a profile in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/) help planners find and book you.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Structure first:** one main message and three supporting points make any talk easier to follow and easier to deliver.
> - **Voice and body language** carry as much of your message as your words. Slow down, pause and stand still when it matters.
> - **Stories and examples** are what audiences remember, so build each point around one.
> - **Improvement comes from a feedback loop:** record, watch, adjust and speak again.

## Where to start: find your biggest gap

Before you work on everything, find the one thing holding you back most. Record yourself giving a five-minute talk on any topic you know well, then watch it with this list:

| Skill area | Ask yourself |
|---|---|
| Structure | Could someone repeat my main message after watching? |
| Voice | Was I easy to hear? Did I vary my pace and tone, or speak too fast? |
| Body language | Did I stand steady, use open gestures and look at the audience? |
| Content | Did I use stories and examples, or only facts and opinions? |
| Filler words | How often did I say "um", "so", "like" or "you know"? |
| Opening and close | Did I start strong and end with a clear message? |

Pick the weakest area and work on it for your next few talks. Then move to the next one.

## 1. Build every talk around one clear message

Most weak talks try to say too much. Before you write anything, finish this sentence: "After my talk, I want the audience to..." That's your main message.

Then use a simple structure:

- **Opening:** a story, question or surprising fact, then why the topic matters to this audience
- **Three main points:** each one supports your message, with an example for each
- **Close:** repeat your message and tell the audience what to do or think next

Three points is enough for most talks under 30 minutes. People remember three far more easily than seven.

## 2. Open strong and close strong

Audiences decide quickly whether to listen. Skip "Thank you for having me, today I'm going to talk about..." and start with something that pulls them in:

- A short story: "Two years ago, I lost our biggest client in a five-minute phone call."
- A question: "How many of you have sat through a meeting that should have been an email?"
- A surprising fact from a source you can name

End with intention. Don't fade out with "So, yeah, that's it." Restate your message in one sentence and give a clear next step, then pause before you say thank you.

## 3. Use your voice on purpose

Your voice can make the same words sound confident or unsure. Work on four things:

- **Pace:** most nervous speakers talk too fast. Slow down, especially on key points.
- **Volume:** speak to the back row. If people lean in to hear you, you've lost them.
- **Variety:** change your pitch and pace to show what matters. A flat tone makes good content sound dull.
- **Pauses:** a pause before an important point builds attention. A pause after it gives people time to think.

Try marking pauses in your notes with a slash, like this: "The fix took five minutes. / The damage took five months to repair."

## 4. Cut filler words

Filler words like "um", "uh", "so" and "like" make you sound less sure, even when you know your topic. You don't need to remove every one, but you can reduce them:

1. Record a practice talk and count your filler words.
2. Notice when they happen, usually between points or when you're thinking.
3. Replace each one with a short pause.
4. Ask a friend to tap the table every time you say one during practice.

Within a few practice sessions, most people cut their filler words by a lot.

## 5. Improve your body language

The audience watches you before they listen to you. Small changes make a big difference:

- **Stand steady:** feet hip-width apart, weight even. Avoid rocking or pacing without a reason.
- **Move with purpose:** walk to a new spot when you start a new point, then stand still.
- **Use open gestures:** keep your hands visible and above your waist. Let them move naturally with what you say.
- **Make eye contact:** look at one person for a full sentence, then move to someone in another part of the room.
- **Face the audience:** don't turn your back to read slides.

## 6. Tell stories, not just facts

People forget statistics and remember stories. For each main point, add one short story or real example. A simple story structure:

1. **Situation:** where and when, in one or two sentences
2. **Problem:** what went wrong or what was at stake
3. **What happened:** the choice or action
4. **Lesson:** how it connects to your point

Your own experiences work best, because no one else can tell them and you'll remember them without notes.

## 7. Make slides support you, not replace you

Slides should help the audience understand, not hold your script. Keep them simple:

- One idea per slide
- A few words or one image, not paragraphs
- Large text that the back row can read
- Charts with one clear takeaway

Your talk should still work if the projector fails. If it doesn't, you're relying on your slides too much.

## 8. Engage your audience

A talk feels shorter and more memorable when the audience takes part. Simple ways to involve them:

- Ask a question and invite a show of hands
- Give them 30 seconds to discuss something with the person next to them
- Use a live poll at virtual or larger events
- Invite one or two people to share a quick example
- Leave time for questions at the end

## 9. Practise the right way

Practice works best when it's specific. A practice plan for an important talk:

| When | What to do |
|---|---|
| Two weeks before | Finish your outline and main stories |
| Ten days before | First full run-through out loud, timed |
| One week before | Record a run and watch it; fix your weakest section |
| Five days before | Practise in front of one or two people and ask for feedback |
| Two days before | Full run-through in the clothes you'll wear, with slides |
| The day before | Practise only your opening and close |
| On the day | Arrive early, check the room, breathe, and run your first line once |

If nerves are your biggest obstacle, our guide on how to build [confidence in public speaking](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-build-confidence-in-public-speaking/) covers that in more detail.

## 10. Get feedback after every talk

You can't improve what you can't see. After each talk:

- Ask the organiser what worked and what could be better
- Ask two or three audience members what they remember most
- Watch the recording if there is one, and write down one strength and one thing to change
- Keep a simple log of each talk with notes, so you can see your progress over time

## 11. Speak more often

The fastest way to improve public speaking is to do more of it. Look for regular chances:

- Volunteer to present in team meetings
- Join a speaking club like Toastmasters
- Speak at local meetups or industry associations
- Run a lunch-and-learn at work
- Host a webinar or go on a podcast in your field

Every talk is practice, and every recording is material you can use later, such as clips for a short [speaker reel](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/make-a-two-minute-speaker-reel-from-footage-you-already-have/).

## Turn better talks into speaking opportunities

As your speaking improves, more people will want to hear you. Event planners look you up before they book, so they need somewhere to see your topics, video and what other organisers said about you.

Speakerfolio writes and builds a free one-page speaker website from your LinkedIn profile, with your talks, video, testimonials and a booking form, on yourname.speakerfolio.com. You're also listed in the Speakerfolio speaker directory, where planners search for speakers. When you want your own domain and a custom design, Premium is $100 a year with hosting and updates included.

## Frequently asked questions

### How can I improve my public speaking quickly?

Focus on one main message with three supporting points, practise out loud at least three times, record one run and fix the biggest problem you see, and replace filler words with pauses.

### What are the most important public speaking skills?

Clear structure, a confident voice with good pace and pauses, open body language, storytelling, and the ability to connect with your audience.

### How do I stop saying "um" when I speak?

Record yourself to see when filler words happen, then practise replacing each one with a short pause. Knowing your structure well also helps, because most filler words appear when you're unsure what comes next.

### How long does it take to get better at public speaking?

Most people see clear progress after a few recorded practice sessions and a handful of real talks. Speaking regularly, even in small settings, is what makes the improvement last.

### Should I use slides when I speak?

Use slides only if they help the audience understand. Keep them simple, with one idea per slide and very little text, and make sure your talk still works without them.

### How do I make my talk more engaging?

Open with a story or question, use real examples for each point, vary your voice, and give the audience a way to take part, such as a show of hands or a short discussion.

### Does joining Toastmasters help with public speaking?

Yes. Speaking clubs like Toastmasters give you regular practice and structured feedback in a supportive setting, which helps many people improve faster.

## Keep improving, one talk at a time

Public speaking improves with focus and repetition. Find your biggest gap, work on it, record yourself and speak again. When you're ready to share your talks with event planners, get your [free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start) from Speakerfolio.

# How to Build Confidence in Public Speaking: 10 Steps That Work

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-build-confidence-in-public-speaking/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**You build confidence in public speaking by preparing well, practising out loud, and speaking often enough that the stage starts to feel familiar.** Nerves don't disappear for most speakers, even professionals. What changes is that you learn to expect them, calm your body, and trust your preparation. Start with small, low-pressure talks, record yourself, and work on one skill at a time. As your confidence grows, a speaker website and a profile in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/) help you turn it into real bookings.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Confidence comes from preparation and repetition**, not from waiting until you stop feeling nervous.
> - **Practise out loud and on video**, not just in your head.
> - **Calm your body first**: slow breathing, a steady stance and a strong first minute make the rest easier.
> - **Speak often on small stages** so big ones feel familiar.

## Why public speaking feels scary

When you stand in front of a group, your body can react as if you are in danger. Your heart beats faster, your hands shake, your mouth goes dry and your mind races. That is your stress response at work. It is normal, and it happens to experienced speakers too.

Most fear of speaking comes from three worries:

- **Being judged:** "They'll think I don't know what I'm talking about."
- **Forgetting:** "My mind will go blank."
- **Losing control:** "My voice will shake and everyone will notice."

Each of these has a practical fix, and that's what the steps below are for.

## How to build confidence in public speaking: 10 steps

### Step 1: Know your material better than your script

Confidence starts with knowing what you want to say. Write down the one main message of your talk in a single sentence. Then list the three to five points that support it. If you know those points well, you can find your way back even if you lose your place.

Don't memorise every word. A memorised script breaks the moment you forget a line. Know your opening and closing by heart, and speak the middle from your key points.

### Step 2: Practise out loud, not in your head

Reading your notes silently feels like practice, but it isn't. Say your talk out loud, standing up, at full volume. You'll find the sentences that are hard to say, the transitions that don't work and how long the talk really takes.

Aim to run through a full talk at least three to five times before an important event.

### Step 3: Record yourself and watch it back

Set up your phone and record a practice run. Watching yourself is uncomfortable at first, but it shows you what the audience sees. Look for one or two things to improve each time, such as:

- Filler words like "um", "so" and "you know"
- Speaking too fast
- Looking at your slides instead of the audience
- Hands in your pockets or fidgeting

You'll usually find you look calmer on video than you felt.

### Step 4: Rehearse in front of real people

Practise in front of a friend, a colleague or a small group. Ask them for one thing that worked and one thing to improve. Having faces in front of you is very different from talking to a wall, and it's the closest thing to the real event.

### Step 5: Prepare a strong first minute

The first minute is when nerves are highest. Plan exactly how you'll start: a short story, a question or a surprising fact, followed by why the topic matters to this audience. When your opening goes well, your body starts to relax and the rest of the talk flows more easily.

### Step 6: Calm your body before you speak

You can't think your way out of a racing heart, but you can breathe your way out of it. Before you go on stage, try slow breathing: breathe in through your nose for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for six. Repeat for a minute or two.

Other things that help:

- Drop your shoulders and unclench your jaw
- Stand with your feet hip-width apart and your weight even
- Drink water, and keep a glass nearby
- Walk around for a few minutes to use up nervous energy

### Step 7: Call your nerves excitement

Nervousness and excitement feel almost the same in your body: fast heartbeat, energy, alertness. A 2014 study by Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks found that people who told themselves "I am excited" before a speech were rated as more persuasive, competent and confident than people who tried to calm down.

Instead of telling yourself to relax, tell yourself you're excited to share something useful.

### Step 8: Focus on the audience, not on yourself

Nerves grow when all your attention is on how you look and sound. Shift your attention to the people in front of you. Ask yourself: what do they need from this talk, and how can I help them?

During the talk, find a few friendly faces in different parts of the room and speak to them one at a time. It feels like a series of conversations instead of a performance.

### Step 9: Plan for what could go wrong

Much of the fear is about what might happen. Decide in advance what you'll do if it does:

| If this happens | Do this |
|---|---|
| Your mind goes blank | Pause, take a breath, look at your notes or repeat your last point |
| Your voice shakes | Slow down, breathe from your belly and lower your pitch slightly |
| Your slides stop working | Keep going from your key points; your talk should work without slides |
| Someone asks a hard question | Thank them, answer what you can, and offer to follow up |
| You make a mistake | Correct it simply and move on; most people won't notice |
| The room feels quiet | Ask a simple question or invite a show of hands |

A pause feels long to you but natural to the audience. Use pauses on purpose and they become a sign of confidence.

### Step 10: Speak often, starting small

Confidence comes from repetition. The more often you speak, the more familiar it feels. Look for low-pressure chances to practise:

- Team meetings and internal presentations
- Local meetups and community groups
- Toastmasters or another speaking club
- Webinars and online events
- Podcasts in your field
- Workshops for small groups

Each talk gives you evidence that you can do it, and that evidence is what confidence is made of. When you're ready to take it further, our guide on how to [become a keynote speaker](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-is-a-keynote-speaker-and-how-to-become-one/) shows the next steps.

## Quick fixes for common nervous signs

| Nervous sign | Quick fix |
|---|---|
| Shaking hands | Hold a clicker or rest your hands lightly on the lectern; use open gestures |
| Fast speech | Mark pauses in your notes and slow down on key points |
| Dry mouth | Sip water before you start and keep a glass on stage |
| Racing heart | Slow breathing for two minutes before you go on |
| Filler words | Replace "um" with a short pause |
| Looking at the floor | Pick three friendly faces in different parts of the room |
| Blank mind | Keep a one-page outline with your key points in large text |

## Your day-of confidence checklist

- Arrive early and see the room before people arrive
- Test the microphone, slides and clicker
- Stand where you'll speak and look out at the seats
- Run through your opening line once, out loud
- Do two minutes of slow breathing
- Put water and your outline where you can reach them
- Smile at the first people who walk in

## How confident speakers turn practice into bookings

Once you've built your confidence, the next challenge is getting invited to speak. Event planners look speakers up online before they book. They want to see your topics, a video of you speaking and what other organisers said about you.

Every talk you give is a chance to collect that proof. Ask organisers if you can record your session, then use the footage to make a short [speaker reel](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/make-a-two-minute-speaker-reel-from-footage-you-already-have/). Ask for a testimonial after each event.

Speakerfolio helps you put all of this in one place. We write and build a free one-page speaker website from your LinkedIn profile, with your talks, video, testimonials and a booking form, on yourname.speakerfolio.com. You're also listed in the Speakerfolio speaker directory, where planners search for speakers. When you want your own domain and a custom design, Premium is $100 a year with hosting and updates included.

## Frequently asked questions

### How can I build confidence in public speaking fast?

Prepare one clear message, practise your talk out loud three to five times, record one run and watch it, and plan a strong opening. On the day, arrive early and do two minutes of slow breathing before you speak.

### Is it normal to be nervous before speaking?

Yes. Most people feel nervous before speaking, including experienced professionals. The goal is not to remove nerves completely but to manage them so they don't get in your way.

### How do I stop my voice from shaking when I speak?

Slow your breathing, breathe from your belly, speak a little slower and slightly lower, and pause between sentences. Sipping water beforehand also helps.

### What should I do if I forget what to say?

Pause, take a breath and look at your notes or outline. You can also repeat your last point or ask the audience a question while you find your place. A short pause looks natural to the audience.

### Should I memorise my speech?

Memorise your opening and closing, but not every word. Speak the middle from your key points so you can recover easily if you lose your place.

### How long does it take to become a confident public speaker?

It depends on how often you speak. Most people notice a real difference after a handful of talks, especially if they record themselves and work on one skill at a time.

### Does joining a speaking club help?

Yes. Clubs like Toastmasters give you regular, low-pressure chances to speak and get feedback, which is one of the fastest ways to build confidence.

## Start building your confidence today

Confidence in public speaking is built one talk at a time. Prepare your message, practise out loud, calm your body and speak as often as you can. When you're ready to get booked, get your [free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start) from Speakerfolio so planners can find you.

# What Does a Keynote Speaker Do? Before, During and After the Event

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-does-a-keynote-speaker-do/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**A keynote speaker gives the main talk at an event and sets the theme for everything that follows.** The talk itself usually lasts 30 to 60 minutes, but most of the work happens around it: learning about the audience, tailoring the stories, checking the stage, then answering questions and following up afterwards. Event planners book keynote speakers to inspire, teach or bring a room together around one idea. You can see what working keynote speakers offer, and book one directly, in the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/).

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **A keynote speaker's main job** is to open or close an event with a talk that frames its theme.
> - **Preparation takes far longer than the talk**: briefing calls, audience research, tailoring and rehearsal.
> - **On the day**, keynote speakers often do more than speak: Q&A, panels, book signings and meeting leaders.
> - **Good keynote speakers follow up**, sharing resources with attendees and checking in with the organiser.

## What does a keynote speaker do, in short?

A keynote speaker delivers the headline talk at a conference, company meeting, summit or awards night. Their talk is the moment the whole audience is in one room, so it has to work for everyone: it sets the mood, introduces the theme and gives people something to talk about for the rest of the event.

To do that, a keynote speaker:

1. Learns what the organiser wants the audience to think, feel or do
2. Shapes their signature talk around that audience and theme
3. Delivers the talk with stories, ideas and practical takeaways
4. Stays involved after the talk through Q&A, extra sessions and follow-up

If you are wondering how people get into this work, our guide on [how to become a keynote speaker](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-is-a-keynote-speaker-and-how-to-become-one/) covers the steps.

## Before the event: what a keynote speaker does to prepare

Most of a keynote speaker's work happens weeks before they walk on stage.

### The briefing call

Once booked, the speaker has a call with the organiser, usually four to six weeks before the event. They ask about:

- Who is in the audience: job roles, seniority, industry and size
- The event theme and the agenda around the keynote
- What has happened in the organisation or industry lately, such as a merger, a new strategy or a hard year
- What success looks like after the talk
- Any topics, words or examples to avoid

### Researching and tailoring

Good keynote speakers don't give the same talk word for word everywhere. They keep the structure of their signature talk and change the examples, stories and language to fit the room. For a sales conference they might use sales examples; for a hospital leadership day, healthcare ones. Some speakers interview a few attendees in advance so they can mention real challenges from the stage.

### Logistics

The speaker or their team confirms:

- Talk length, start time and where it sits in the agenda
- Stage setup, microphone type (handheld, headset or lapel) and screen size
- Slides, video and any props
- Travel, accommodation and arrival time
- Whether the session will be recorded or streamed

### Helping promote the event

Many organisers ask keynote speakers to share the event with their own audience. That can mean a social post, a short video invitation or an interview for the event newsletter.

## On the day: what a keynote speaker does at the event

### Tech check and rehearsal

A keynote speaker usually arrives early to walk the stage, test the microphone, check the slides on the big screen and agree cues with the event's technical team.

### Delivering the keynote

This is the part everyone sees. A strong keynote usually:

- Opens with a story or moment that pulls the room in
- Names a problem the audience recognises
- Offers one clear idea, framework or way of thinking
- Backs it up with stories, examples and results
- Ends with something the audience can use or remember

### Q&A and extra sessions

Many keynotes end with 10 to 15 minutes of questions. Depending on the booking, the speaker may also:

- Join a panel later in the day
- Run a smaller breakout session or workshop
- Sign and sell books
- Meet sponsors, VIPs or the leadership team
- Give interviews to the event's media team

### A sample day for a keynote speaker

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 7:30 | Arrive at the venue, meet the event manager |
| 7:45 | Sound check, microphone fitting and slide check on stage |
| 8:30 | Breakfast with the organisers and leadership team |
| 9:15 | Opening keynote (45 minutes) |
| 10:00 | Q&A with the audience (15 minutes) |
| 10:30 | Book signing and conversations with attendees |
| 13:30 | Join an afternoon panel |
| 15:00 | Leave for the airport |

## After the event: what a keynote speaker does next

The work doesn't end when the applause does. Good keynote speakers:

- **Send resources** promised from the stage, such as slides, a checklist or a workbook
- **Check in with the organiser** to hear what landed and what attendees said
- **Ask for a testimonial** while the event is still fresh
- **Share the event** on social media and thank the organisers publicly
- **Offer follow-up** like workshops or coaching if the organisation wants to go deeper

## Types of keynotes and what each one does

| Type of keynote | When it happens | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Opening keynote | Start of the event | Sets the theme and energy for the day |
| Closing keynote | End of the event | Pulls ideas together and sends people off with a clear message |
| Lunch or after-dinner keynote | Middle or evening | Re-energises the room, often with more humour and story |
| Corporate kick-off keynote | Start of a year or quarter | Aligns teams behind a new strategy or goal |
| Awards night keynote | During a celebration | Inspires and honours achievement |
| Virtual keynote | Online event or webinar | Delivers the same role on camera, with more interaction to hold attention |

## What event organisers expect from a keynote speaker

When planners book a keynote speaker, they expect more than a good talk. They want someone who:

- Understands their audience and makes the talk feel written for them
- Arrives on time, prepared and easy to work with
- Sticks to the agreed length
- Sets the right tone for the event and the organisation
- Gives the audience ideas they can actually use
- Responds quickly before and after the event

If you are a planner looking for someone who fits that list, our guide on [how to find a keynote speaker](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-find-a-keynote-speaker/) walks through the process step by step.

## How keynote speakers get booked

Before a planner books a keynote speaker, they look them up. They search the speaker's name, ask AI assistants for speakers on their topic and browse speaker directories. What they want to find is simple: the speaker's topics, a stage video, testimonials from other organisers and a way to check availability.

That's why most working keynote speakers have a speaker website and a profile in a speaker directory. Without them, planners have very little to go on.

## Frequently asked questions

### What does a keynote speaker do?

A keynote speaker gives the main talk at an event, usually at the start or end. They set the theme, prepare by learning about the audience, tailor their talk, deliver it and often take questions and follow up afterwards.

### How long does a keynote speech last?

Most keynote speeches last 30 to 60 minutes. Many end with 10 to 15 minutes of questions from the audience.

### What is the purpose of a keynote speaker?

The purpose is to bring the whole audience together around one idea or theme, set the tone for the event and give people something useful or inspiring to take away.

### How does a keynote speaker prepare for an event?

They have a briefing call with the organiser, research the audience, tailor their stories and examples, confirm the stage and technical setup, and rehearse. Many also arrive early on the day for a sound and slide check.

### Does a keynote speaker do anything besides the main talk?

Often, yes. Depending on the booking, a keynote speaker may answer questions, join a panel, run a workshop, sign books or meet the leadership team.

### What is the difference between a keynote speaker and a guest speaker?

A keynote speaker gives the main talk that frames the whole event. A guest speaker can be anyone invited to speak, often in a shorter or smaller session.

### How do I find and book a keynote speaker?

Start with your event goal, audience and budget, then search speaker directories, speakers bureaus and referrals. Watch each speaker's video, read their testimonials and contact your shortlist through their website or directory profile.

## Find or become a keynote speaker

A keynote speaker does far more than talk for 45 minutes. They prepare around your audience, set the tone on the day and help the ideas last after the event.

If you are planning an event, browse the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/). If you are a speaker, get your [free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start) built and listed today.

# What Is a Keynote Speaker? How to Become a Keynote Speaker in 9 Steps

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-is-a-keynote-speaker-and-how-to-become-one/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**A keynote speaker is the person an event books to open or close it with a main talk that sets the theme for everyone in the room.** Keynotes usually run 30 to 60 minutes, and they go to people with real expertise and a story worth hearing. To become a keynote speaker, pick one topic you know deeply, build a signature talk around it, practise on smaller stages, collect video and testimonials, and make yourself easy to find with a speaker website. Speakerfolio builds that website for you for free and lists you in its [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/), where planners search for speakers.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **A keynote speaker** delivers the main talk at an event and sets the tone for the rest of the programme.
> - **You don't need fame** to start. You need one clear topic, one strong talk and proof that you can hold a room.
> - **Most speakers start small**: free talks at meetups, associations and company events, then paid local keynotes.
> - **Planners check you online before they book**, so a speaker website with your talks, video and a booking form matters early on.

## What is a keynote speaker?

A keynote speaker gives the headline talk at a conference, company meeting, summit or awards night. The word comes from music, where the keynote is the note a piece is built around. A keynote talk does the same job for an event: it sets the theme that the other sessions follow.

Most keynotes are 30 to 60 minutes long and happen at the start of the event (the opening keynote) or at the end (the closing keynote). Some events also book a keynote for after lunch or dinner, when the room needs energy.

A keynote speaker is usually one of these:

- **An expert** in a field such as leadership, sales, health, technology or education
- **A practitioner** who has done something the audience wants to learn from, like building a company or leading a team through a crisis
- **A storyteller** with a personal experience that carries a lesson, such as an athlete, survivor or adventurer
- **An author** whose book gives the talk its framework

## What does a keynote speaker do?

The talk is the visible part. Most of a keynote speaker's work happens before and after it.

**Before the event**, a keynote speaker talks to the organiser about the audience and goals, tailors examples and stories to that audience, prepares slides or visuals and checks the stage, sound and timing.

**On the day**, they deliver the talk, often answer questions, and sometimes stay for a book signing, a panel or a dinner with leaders.

**After the event**, they follow up with the organiser, share resources with attendees and ask for a testimonial.

## Keynote speaker vs other types of speakers

| Speaker type | What they do | Typical length |
|---|---|---|
| Keynote speaker | Gives the main talk that sets the event's theme | 30 to 60 minutes |
| Breakout or session speaker | Leads a smaller session on one subtopic | 30 to 60 minutes |
| Workshop leader or trainer | Runs hands-on learning with exercises | Half day to full day |
| Panelist | Shares views in a moderated discussion with others | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Emcee or host | Introduces speakers and keeps the event on schedule | Whole event |
| Motivational speaker | Focuses on inspiration and mindset, often as a keynote | 30 to 60 minutes |

Many keynote speakers also offer workshops or virtual talks, which gives organisers more ways to book them.

## Do you need to be famous to be a keynote speaker?

No. Celebrity speakers get the biggest fees, but most keynotes go to people who are known in one industry or on one topic. A regional sales director with a clear method for coaching teams can be the perfect keynote for a sales kick-off. A nurse who led a ward through a hospital merger can be the right keynote for a healthcare conference.

What planners look for is fit: the right topic for their audience, proof that you speak well, and confidence that you will be easy to work with.

## How to become a keynote speaker: 9 steps

### Step 1: Pick one topic you can own

Choose a topic where your experience is real and specific. "Leadership" is too wide. "How first-time managers keep their best people during change" is a topic a planner can picture on their agenda.

Ask yourself three questions:

1. What do people already ask me for advice about?
2. What have I done or lived through that others want to learn from?
3. Which audiences need this, and do they hold events?

### Step 2: Know your audience

Write down who your talk is for: their job, industry, seniority and the problem they face. The narrower the audience, the easier it is for planners in that space to say yes. You can widen it later.

### Step 3: Build a signature talk

Your signature talk is the one you will give again and again, adapted for each event. A simple structure works:

- **Opening:** a story or moment that pulls the audience in
- **The problem:** what your audience struggles with and why it matters
- **Your idea:** a framework, method or lesson, usually in three to five parts
- **Stories and proof:** examples, results and moments from your own experience
- **Close:** what the audience should think, feel or do next

Give the talk a clear title and promise, such as "Lead Through Change: How Managers Keep Teams Focused When Everything Moves".

### Step 4: Practise on smaller stages

Every keynote speaker starts somewhere small. Good first stages include:

- Industry meetups and networking groups
- Professional associations and chambers of commerce
- Your own company's team meetings and offsites
- Webinars and online summits
- Podcasts in your field
- Universities and alumni events

Speak for free at first if it gets you in front of the right audience. Ask every organiser if you can record the talk.

### Step 5: Record your talks and make a speaker reel

Video is often the first thing a planner wants to see. Record every talk you can, even on a phone at the back of the room. Then cut your best moments into a two-to-three-minute speaker reel. Our guide to making a [speaker reel](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/make-a-two-minute-speaker-reel-from-footage-you-already-have/) shows how to do it from footage you already have.

### Step 6: Collect testimonials

After each talk, ask the organiser for two or three sentences about what changed for their audience. A quote with a name, job title and organisation carries much more weight than an anonymous one. Collect attendee feedback too.

### Step 7: Write your speaker bio and one-sheet

Planners need a short bio they can print in the programme and read out before you walk on stage. Write a 50-word and a 150-word version that say who you are, what you speak about and why you are credible. Then put your bio, talk titles, photo and contact details on a one-page speaker sheet. Our guide to writing a [speaker bio](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-write-a-speaker-bio-planners-can-actually-use/) walks through it.

### Step 8: Get a speaker website

When a planner hears your name, they search for you. They also ask AI assistants like ChatGPT for speakers on their topic. If all they find is a social profile, it is hard for them to judge you and easy to move on to someone else.

A speaker website brings everything together in one place:

- Your topic and who you help
- Your signature talks and what audiences take away
- Your speaker reel
- Testimonials from organisers
- Past events and logos
- Your bio and photos
- A booking form

A clear website also helps Google and AI assistants understand who you are and what you speak about. It cannot guarantee a ranking or a recommendation, but it makes both far more likely than a social profile alone.

### Step 9: Start pitching and set your fees

With a talk, video, testimonials and a website, you can start contacting event organisers. Look for events your audience attends, find the person who books speakers and send a short, specific pitch with a link to your website.

As you gain experience, start charging. Fees vary a lot by experience and industry. Many speakers start with local and nonprofit events and raise their fees as demand grows.

| Speaker level | Typical fee per keynote |
|---|---|
| New speaker | Free to $1,500 |
| Emerging speaker | $1,500 to $5,000 |
| Established professional | $5,000 to $30,000 |
| Celebrity or bestselling author | $30,000 to $100,000+ |

## Skills every keynote speaker needs

- **Storytelling:** turning experience into stories with a clear point
- **Stage presence:** voice, pace, movement and eye contact
- **Audience awareness:** reading the room and adjusting as you go
- **Tailoring:** adapting one talk to different industries and goals
- **Reliability:** being on time, prepared and easy to work with
- **Self-promotion:** sharing your work so the right people know you exist

You can improve all of them. Groups like Toastmasters, speaking coaches and watching your own recordings all help.

## Common mistakes new keynote speakers make

- Choosing a topic so broad that no planner knows where to place them
- Writing a new talk for every event instead of refining one signature talk
- Not recording talks, then having no video when a planner asks
- Forgetting to ask for testimonials while the event is still fresh
- Relying only on LinkedIn or Instagram instead of having a proper speaker website
- Pitching events without a clear link that shows talks, video and how to book

Speakerfolio builds websites for speakers, trainers and coaches. It goes live on yourname.speakerfolio.com, usually within two working days, and it costs nothing.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a keynote speaker?

A keynote speaker gives the main talk at an event, usually at the start or end. The keynote sets the theme for the event and typically lasts 30 to 60 minutes.

### How do I become a keynote speaker with no experience?

Pick one topic you know well, build a signature talk, and practise at meetups, associations, webinars and company events. Record your talks, collect testimonials and create a speaker website so planners can find and book you.

### How long does it take to become a keynote speaker?

It depends on your topic, network and how often you speak. Many people get their first paid keynote after giving a series of free or low-fee talks and building video and testimonials along the way.

### How much do keynote speakers get paid?

New speakers often start free or under $1,500. Emerging speakers usually charge $1,500 to $5,000, established professionals $5,000 to $30,000, and celebrities $30,000 or more per keynote.

### Do keynote speakers need a website?

Yes. Planners search speakers online before booking. A speaker website shows your talks, video, testimonials and booking form in one place, and it helps Google and AI assistants understand what you speak about.

### What is the difference between a keynote speaker and a motivational speaker?

A keynote speaker is defined by their role at the event: giving the main talk. A motivational speaker is defined by their style: inspiring the audience. Many motivational speakers are booked as keynote speakers.

### Can I be a keynote speaker part time?

Yes. Many keynote speakers have full-time careers and speak a few times a year. Their day job is often what makes them credible on their topic.

## Start your keynote speaking career

Becoming a keynote speaker starts with one topic, one strong talk and the proof that you can deliver it. Practise on small stages, record everything, collect testimonials and give planners an easy way to find you.
