# How to Find a Keynote Speaker: 9 Steps to the Right Speaker for Your Event

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-find-a-keynote-speaker/
Published: 2026-11-19 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**To find a keynote speaker, start with your event goal and audience, set a realistic budget, then search the places planners trust most: online [speaker directories](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/) such as Speakerfolio, speakers bureaus, referrals from other organizers and speakers you have already seen live.** Build a shortlist of five to eight names, watch real stage video for each one, read testimonials from other event organizers and send a short brief to your top three. Most planners can find a keynote speaker in two to four weeks this way, and the best speakers should be contacted six to nine months before the event.

This guide shows you how to find a keynote speaker step by step, with a brief template, an outreach email and a scorecard you can copy.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Start with the outcome**, not a famous name. Write down what the audience should think, feel or do after the keynote.
> - **The fastest place to find a keynote speaker** is a speaker directory where every profile shows topics, video, testimonials and a booking form side by side.
> - **Shortlist five to eight speakers**, then cut to three using video, organizer testimonials and topic fit.
> - **Contact speakers six to nine months ahead** with a one-page brief that includes your date, audience, format and budget range.

## Step 1: Define what your keynote speaker needs to achieve

Before you search, decide what success looks like. The keynote usually sets the tone for the whole event, so a speaker who is brilliant in the wrong way can still be the wrong choice.

Answer these five questions in one sentence each:

1. **Who is the audience?** Job roles, seniority, industry and size. "300 regional sales managers" leads to a very different speaker than "1,200 nurses".
2. **What is the event theme?** The keynote should frame it, not compete with it.
3. **What should people take away?** For example: "Leave confident about leading through change."
4. **What is the format?** Opening keynote, closing keynote, after-dinner talk or virtual session, and how long.
5. **What tone fits the room?** Inspiring, practical, funny, data-driven or a mix.

These answers become your search filters. They also become the brief you send speakers later, so the time is not wasted.

## Step 2: Set a realistic budget

Your budget decides which channels are worth your time. Searching celebrity bureaus with a $3,000 budget wastes weeks, and so does sorting through new speakers when you need a household name.

| Speaker level | Typical fee per keynote | Where to find them |
|---|---|---|
| Emerging speaker | $1,500 to $5,000 | Speaker directories, referrals, local associations |
| Established professional | $5,000 to $30,000 | Speaker directories, speakers bureaus, direct outreach |
| Celebrity or bestselling author | $30,000 to $100,000+ | Speakers bureaus, agents |

Remember to add travel, accommodation and audio-visual costs, which are usually paid on top of the fee. For a full breakdown of fees and how to get more value from your budget, read our guide to [keynote speakers for hire](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/keynote-speakers-for-hire/).

## Step 3: Search the right places to find a keynote speaker

There are five reliable ways to find a keynote speaker. Most planners use two or three of them together.

| Where to look | Best for | Speed | Cost to search |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speaker directories | Comparing many speakers by topic and format | Fast | Free |
| Speakers bureaus | Large budgets and high-demand names | Fast once briefed | Commission built into the fee |
| Referrals from other planners | Proven speakers for similar audiences | Medium | Free |
| Speakers you have seen live | Knowing exactly how they perform | Slow | Free |
| Google, LinkedIn and AI assistants | Niche topics and local speakers | Medium | Free |

### Speaker directories

A speaker directory is the quickest way to find a keynote speaker when you know your topic but not the name. You can filter by subject, format and location, then compare profiles side by side and contact speakers directly without an agency fee.

The quality of a directory depends on how complete each profile is. A list of names and headshots does not help you decide. Look for a directory where every speaker shows their talks, a stage video, testimonials and a clear way to book.

That is why we built the Speakerfolio [speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/). Every speaker has a full website and a profile built on the same structure: who they help, their talk titles, video, testimonials from organizers and a booking form that goes straight to them. You can compare speakers in minutes instead of opening twenty tabs, and searching is always free.

### Speakers bureaus

A speakers bureau represents many speakers and handles shortlisting, negotiation and contracts for you. Bureaus are useful for big events, tight deadlines and famous names. The trade-off is cost: the bureau's commission, often 20% to 30%, is built into the speaker's fee, and many bureaus focus on speakers above $10,000.

### Referrals from other planners

Ask planners in your industry, association or LinkedIn network who they booked recently and whether they would book them again. A referral tells you something no profile can: how the speaker behaved behind the scenes, how well they tailored the talk and how the audience responded.

### Speakers you have seen live

If you have seen a speaker hold a room at another event, you already know their stage presence. Note their name, then check their website for current topics and availability.

### Google, LinkedIn and AI assistants

Searching "leadership keynote speaker Chicago" or asking an AI assistant for speakers on a niche topic can surface people who are not with a bureau. Results vary, though. Speakers with a proper website, clear topics and a directory profile are much easier to find and check this way than speakers with only a social media page.

## Step 4: Build a shortlist of five to eight speakers

Aim for five to eight names. Fewer than five gives you no backup if your first choice is unavailable. More than eight turns vetting into a part-time job.

For each speaker, capture the same details in one place:

- Name and link to their website or profile
- Main keynote topic and talk title
- Formats offered (in person, virtual, workshop)
- Link to a stage video
- Fee range, if listed
- Location and travel needs

When every speaker shows the same information in the same order, this step takes minutes. That is the main reason planners start with a directory that uses standardized profiles.

## Step 5: Vet each keynote speaker in 30 minutes

You do not need hours per speaker. Thirty focused minutes tells you most of what you need to know.

1. **Watch real stage video (10 minutes).** Look for footage from a live event with an audience, not a studio clip. Watch the opening and a middle section. Do they hold attention? Would this style suit your room?
2. **Read organizer testimonials (5 minutes).** Quotes from event organizers matter more than quotes from attendees. Look for names, job titles and organizations.
3. **Check past events (5 minutes).** Have they spoken to audiences like yours, in your industry or at your event size?
4. **Review their talks (5 minutes).** Is there a talk that matches your theme, or will they need to build something new?
5. **Look at their website (5 minutes).** A clear, up-to-date speaker website with talks, video and a booking form is a good sign of how organized they will be to work with. Our [leadership speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-event-planners-look-for-on-a-leadership-speaker-website/) checklist explains what a strong one includes.

### Red flags when you find a keynote speaker

- No video of them speaking to a live audience
- Testimonials with no names or organizations
- A website or profile that has not been updated in years
- A generic talk that cannot be tailored to your audience
- Slow or vague replies to a simple availability question

## Step 6: Compare your finalists with a scorecard

Cut your shortlist to three, then score each speaker from 1 to 5 on the same criteria. This keeps the decision objective and makes it easy to explain to your team or client.

| Criteria | Weight | Speaker A | Speaker B | Speaker C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Topic fit with your theme | 25% | | | |
| Stage presence on video | 25% | | | |
| Organizer testimonials | 15% | | | |
| Experience with similar audiences | 15% | | | |
| Willingness to tailor the talk | 10% | | | |
| Fee within budget | 10% | | | |

Multiply each score by its weight and add them up. The highest total is usually your speaker, but if two are close, a short call will decide it.

## Step 7: Contact speakers with a clear brief

Speakers reply faster, and give you better answers, when your first message has everything they need. Send it to your top two or three at the same time.

Here is an example outreach email. Swap in your own event details:

> **Subject:** Keynote enquiry: Northstar Sales Summit, 14 May, Chicago
>
> Hi Maya,
>
> I'm organizing the Northstar Sales Summit, a one-day conference for 300 regional sales leaders in Chicago on 14 May. We're looking for a 45-minute opening keynote on leading through change, and your talk "Steady Hands in Shaky Markets" looks like a strong fit.
>
> Our budget for the keynote is $8,000 to $12,000, plus travel. Could you let me know if you're available, and whether you could tailor the talk to our audience?
>
> Thanks,
> Daniel Reyes, Events Manager, +1 312 555 0148

Including a budget range saves both sides time. If you contact speakers through a directory booking form, add the same details to the message.

## Step 8: Hold a short call before you book

A 20-minute call shows you how the speaker thinks, listens and adapts. Ask:

- How would you tailor this talk to our audience and theme?
- What do you need from us before the event?
- What audio-visual setup do you need?
- Can we record the session or share your slides?
- Will you stay for a Q&A, a book signing or networking?
- What is your cancellation and rescheduling policy?

If the answers are specific and the speaker asks good questions about your audience, you have probably found your keynote speaker.

## Step 9: Confirm the booking in writing

Once you have chosen, confirm everything in a written agreement. It should cover the fee and deposit, date and time, talk length and format, travel and accommodation, recording rights, audio-visual needs and the cancellation policy. Most speakers ask for a deposit of around 50% to hold the date.

After signing, book a prep call four to six weeks before the event to share audience details, the agenda and any last-minute changes.

## How long does it take to find a keynote speaker?

With a clear brief and a good speaker directory, most planners can find a keynote speaker in two to four weeks. The search itself is fast. Waiting for replies and comparing finalists takes longer. Contact speakers six to nine months before your event, or nine to twelve months for high-demand names and peak conference months.

| Step | Time needed |
|---|---|
| Define goals and budget | 1 to 2 days |
| Search and shortlist | 2 to 5 days |
| Vet and score finalists | 2 to 3 days |
| Outreach and replies | 1 to 2 weeks |
| Call and contract | 3 to 7 days |

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I find a keynote speaker for my event?

Define your audience, theme and goal first, then set a budget. Search speaker directories such as Speakerfolio, speakers bureaus and referrals from other planners. Shortlist five to eight speakers, watch their stage video, read organizer testimonials and contact your top three with a short brief.

### Where is the best place to find a keynote speaker?

For most events, a speaker directory is the fastest place to find a keynote speaker because you can compare topics, video, testimonials and booking details side by side for free. Speakers bureaus are better for celebrity speakers and very large budgets.

### How much does it cost to book a keynote speaker?

Emerging keynote speakers usually charge $1,500 to $5,000, established professionals $5,000 to $30,000, and celebrities $30,000 to $100,000 or more. Travel, accommodation and audio-visual costs are usually extra.

### How far in advance should I find a keynote speaker?

Start looking six to nine months before your event. For high-demand speakers, popular dates or large conferences, start nine to twelve months ahead.

### How can I tell if a keynote speaker is good?

Watch video of them speaking to a live audience, read testimonials from event organizers, check that they have spoken to similar audiences and hold a short call to see how well they tailor their talk.

### Can I find a keynote speaker without a speakers bureau?

Yes. Many professional speakers take bookings directly through their website or a speaker directory. Booking directly usually avoids agency commission, though you will handle the contract and logistics yourself.

### Can AI help me find a keynote speaker?

AI assistants can suggest speakers for a topic or location, but they only recommend speakers they can find information about online. Always check the speaker's website, video and testimonials before you reach out.

## Find your keynote speaker today

Knowing how to find a keynote speaker comes down to a clear goal, the right search channels and a simple, consistent way to compare. Define the outcome you want, shortlist speakers with complete profiles, judge them on real stage video and organizer feedback, and contact your favourites early with a clear brief.

# Keynote Speakers for Hire: How to Find, Vet and Book the Right Speaker

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/keynote-speakers-for-hire/
Published: 2026-11-17 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

**Keynote speakers for hire are professional presenters you pay to open, anchor or close an event with a talk built around your theme and audience.** You can find them in three main places: speakers bureaus, online speaker directories such as [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/), and direct outreach to speakers you already know about. Most professional keynote speakers charge between $5,000 and $30,000 per talk plus travel, and the best ones should be booked six to nine months ahead. To choose well, check four things before anything else: topic fit, a real stage video, testimonials from event organizers and a clear way to send a booking request.

This guide walks you through each step, from building a shortlist to signing the contract, so you can hire with confidence and spend hours, not weeks, doing it.

> **Key takeaways**
>
> - **Where to look:** speakers bureaus (full service, highest cost), speaker directories (fast, free to search) and direct outreach (cheapest, slowest).
> - **What it costs:** about $1,500 to $5,000 for emerging speakers, $5,000 to $30,000 for established professionals, and $30,000 to $100,000+ for celebrities.
> - **When to book:** six to nine months ahead for most events, nine to twelve months or more for high-demand names.
> - **How to vet:** watch real stage footage, read testimonials from organizers, confirm past events and get a one-sheet before you talk money.

## What is a keynote speaker for hire?

A keynote speaker is the featured presenter who sets the tone for an event. The keynote usually runs 30 to 60 minutes, is delivered to the full audience in a general session and ties directly to the event's theme. A keynote speaker "for hire" is simply a speaker who takes paid engagements, either directly or through an agent.

Keynotes are different from other session types, and the difference affects what you should look for and what you should pay.

| Session type | Typical length | Audience | Main goal | What to look for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Keynote | 30 to 60 minutes | Whole event | Inspire and frame the theme | Stage presence, storytelling, a memorable message |
| Breakout session | 45 to 90 minutes | A smaller group | Teach a specific skill | Subject expertise, practical takeaways |
| Workshop | 2 hours to a full day | Small, hands-on group | Build capability | Facilitation skills, materials, exercises |
| Panel or moderated talk | 30 to 60 minutes | Whole event or track | Debate and insight | Quick thinking, comfort with questions |
| Virtual keynote | 20 to 45 minutes | Online attendees | Engage a remote audience | Camera presence, good audio and video setup |

Many speakers offer more than one format. A leadership speaker might deliver a 45-minute keynote in the morning and a half-day workshop in the afternoon, which can be better value than booking two different people.

## Where to find keynote speakers for hire

There is no single right channel. The best one depends on your budget, timeline and how much of the work you want to do yourself.

| Channel | Best for | Cost to you | Speed | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speakers bureau | Large budgets, celebrity or high-demand names | Commission is built into the fee | Fast once briefed | Many bureaus focus on speakers above $10,000 |
| Speaker directory | Browsing many speakers quickly by topic | Usually free to search | Fast | Profile quality varies between directories |
| Direct outreach | Speakers you already know or have seen | No middleman | Slow | You handle contracts and logistics yourself |
| Referrals from peers | Proven speakers for similar audiences | No middleman | Medium | A smaller pool to choose from |
| Associations and industry events | Niche expertise for specialist audiences | Varies | Medium | Experts are not always polished presenters |

### Speakers bureaus

A speakers bureau is an agency that represents many speakers and matches them to events. Bureaus shortlist speakers, negotiate fees and handle contracts, which saves you time. In return they take a commission from the speaker's fee. In an interview with SpeakerFlow, a bureau owner put it plainly: "Most bureaus are going to be charging a 25% commission" ([SpeakerFlow](https://speakerflow.com/how-does-a-speakers-bureau-work/)). Rates of 20% to 30% are common across the industry.

Because a bureau earns a percentage, some will not take bookings under about $10,000. If your budget is smaller, a directory or direct outreach usually works better.

### Speaker directories

A speaker directory lets you search many speakers in one place, filter by topic, format and location, then contact the ones you like. The big advantage is speed: you can compare a dozen speakers in an afternoon instead of chasing a dozen separate websites.

The weakness is inconsistency. On many directories, one speaker has a full profile with video and testimonials while the next has a headshot and two lines of text. That is why the structure of a directory matters as much as its size. On [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/), every speaker profile follows the same layout, with topics, formats, a stage video, organizer testimonials, past events and a booking form, so you can compare speakers like for like. Planners search for free and contact speakers directly, with no booking fee.

### Direct outreach

If you already know who you want, contact the speaker through their website or LinkedIn. You avoid commissions, but you take on the negotiation, contract and travel planning yourself. Direct booking works best for experienced planners or for speakers who manage their own bookings.

## How much does it cost to hire a keynote speaker?

Keynote fees vary widely, but most speakers fall into recognisable tiers. The ranges below come from the National Speakers Bureau's published fee guide ([NSB](https://www.nsb.com/blog/how-much-does-a-keynote-speaker-cost-a-clear-guide-for-event-planners/)).

| Speaker tier | Typical fee per keynote | Who they are |
|---|---|---|
| Entry level | $1,500 to $5,000 | Emerging speakers, subject experts and local professionals |
| Mid-range | $5,000 to $15,000 | Experienced speakers with a track record and strong reviews |
| Professional | $15,000 to $30,000 | Established names, published authors and in-demand industry voices |
| Celebrity | $30,000 to $100,000+ | Famous athletes, executives, authors and public figures |

### What affects a speaker's fee

- **Expertise and demand.** Rare knowledge on a trending topic costs more.
- **Experience.** Seasoned speakers with proven results charge more than newcomers.
- **Event type.** Corporate events often pay more than non-profit or education events.
- **Travel and timing.** Long-haul and international travel usually raises the fee.
- **Format and length.** Adding a workshop, a book signing or a second session increases the total.

### Costs beyond the speaking fee

Budget for these separately, because they are rarely included in the quoted fee:

- **Travel:** flights, ground transport and hotel, usually paid by the client.
- **Meals and incidentals** during the stay.
- **Audio-visual requirements** listed in the speaker's tech rider.
- **Books or materials** for attendees, if you want them.
- **Recording rights** if you plan to share the talk after the event.

A good rule: add 10% to 20% on top of the speaking fee for travel and extras when you set your budget.

### How to get more value from your budget

- **Book early.** Speakers have more flexibility on fees when their calendar is open.
- **Combine sessions.** Ask for a keynote plus a breakout or workshop on the same day.
- **Go virtual.** Remote keynotes remove travel costs and are often priced lower.
- **Consider rising speakers.** Many mid-range speakers deliver as well as famous names for a fraction of the fee, especially on specialist topics.

## How to vet a keynote speaker in 30 minutes

A polished website does not prove a speaker can hold a room. Use this checklist to judge real ability quickly. If a speaker's profile has everything below in one place, vetting takes minutes rather than hours.

1. **Topic fit.** Read their talk titles and descriptions. Do they solve the exact challenge your audience faces? A strong speaker explains who each talk is for and what attendees will take away.
2. **Real stage video.** Watch at least five minutes of genuine footage from a live event, not just a highlight montage. Look at pace, energy, humour and how the audience reacts.
3. **Organizer testimonials.** Quotes from event planners and conference leads matter more than praise from attendees. Look for specifics: did the speaker customise the talk, stay on time and work well with the team?
4. **Past events.** Check the organizations and audiences they have spoken to. Similar industries and audience sizes are a good sign.
5. **A one-sheet and bio.** Professional speakers have a one-page summary with topics, bio, photos and formats ready to send. It shows they are easy to work with.
6. **Booking clarity.** Is there a clear way to check availability and send a request? A speaker who is hard to reach before the booking will be hard to reach after it.
7. **A short fit call.** Before you sign, spend 15 to 20 minutes on a call. Ask how they would tailor the talk to your audience and listen for questions about your event.

### Red flags to watch for

- No real video, or only a 30-second reel made of stock footage.
- Testimonials with no names, roles or organizations.
- Vague topics such as "motivation" with no clear outcome.
- Slow or unclear replies during the enquiry stage.
- Pressure to sign quickly without a written agreement.

## The speaker booking process, step by step

Here is a simple process that works for most corporate events, conferences and association meetings.

1. **Define the goal (9 to 12 months out).** Write one sentence on what the audience should think, feel or do after the keynote.
2. **Set the budget.** Include the fee, travel and extras, and agree on a maximum.
3. **Build a longlist (6 to 9 months out).** Use a directory, a bureau or referrals to find eight to ten candidates.
4. **Shortlist three speakers.** Apply the vetting checklist above and compare them side by side.
5. **Check availability and fees.** Send a short brief with your date, location, audience size and format.
6. **Hold a fit call.** Speak to your top choice and confirm they can tailor the talk.
7. **Sign the contract.** Agree on the fee, deposit, travel, cancellation terms, recording rights and tech needs in writing.
8. **Prepare together.** Share audience insights, the agenda and your event theme. Schedule a tech check before the day.

How far ahead should you start? Leading Authorities, a major speakers bureau, recommends booking most keynote speakers "6 to 9 months" before the event and starting nine to twelve months or more ahead for high-demand names, because calendars fill fast during the spring and autumn conference seasons ([Leading Authorities](https://www.leadingauthorities.com/blog/how-far-in-advance-should-you-book-a-keynote-speaker)). Booking with less than three months' notice is possible, but you will need a few backup options ready.

## Questions to ask before you book a keynote speaker

Send these questions before the contract stage. The answers reveal how professional and flexible a speaker is.

- How will you tailor this talk to our industry and audience?
- Can you share a full, unedited recording of a recent keynote?
- Who is a past client we could speak to as a reference?
- What is included in your fee, and what is billed separately?
- What are your audio-visual and stage requirements?
- Do you offer a workshop, breakout or virtual option as well?
- What is your cancellation and rescheduling policy?
- Can we record the session and share it with attendees afterwards?

## How to compare keynote speakers side by side

When you have three finalists, score each one on the same criteria. A simple scorecard removes guesswork and makes the decision easy to explain to your committee or leadership team.

| Criteria | Weight | Speaker A | Speaker B | Speaker C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Topic fit with our theme | 30% | | | |
| Stage presence on video | 25% | | | |
| Organizer testimonials | 15% | | | |
| Relevant past events | 10% | | | |
| Fee within budget | 10% | | | |
| Ease of communication | 10% | | | |

Score each line from one to five, multiply by the weight and add up the totals. The highest score usually wins, but trust your fit call if two speakers are close.

## Why standardized speaker portfolios save planners hours

Most of the time spent hiring a keynote speaker goes on hunting for basic information. One speaker keeps their topics on a website, their video on YouTube, their testimonials in a PDF and their fee in an email. Another has a beautiful site with no video at all. Comparing them means opening dozens of tabs and filling a spreadsheet by hand.

Standardized speaker portfolios fix this. When every speaker presents the same information in the same order, you can compare them in minutes. Look for directories and speaker websites that show:

- **Who the speaker helps** and the outcome of each talk.
- **Talk titles** with formats and lengths.
- **A real stage video** you can watch on the page.
- **Organizer testimonials** with names and organizations.
- **Past events** and audience types.
- **A booking form** that goes straight to the speaker.

This is the idea behind [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/). Every speaker in the directory has a full website and a profile built on the same structure, so you can filter by topic and format, watch the video, read the proof and send a request in one place. For a closer look at what a strong speaker website includes, read [what event planners look for on a leadership speaker's website](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-event-planners-look-for-on-a-leadership-speaker-website/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I find keynote speakers for hire?

You can find keynote speakers for hire through speakers bureaus, online speaker directories, referrals from other planners and direct outreach on LinkedIn or speaker websites. Directories such as Speakerfolio let you filter speakers by topic and format and contact them directly for free.

### How much does it cost to hire a keynote speaker?

Most professional keynote speakers charge between $5,000 and $30,000 per talk. Emerging speakers often charge $1,500 to $5,000, while celebrities can charge $30,000 to $100,000 or more. Travel, accommodation and audio-visual needs are usually paid separately.

### How far in advance should I book a keynote speaker?

Book most keynote speakers six to nine months before your event. For high-demand or celebrity speakers, start nine to twelve months or more ahead, especially for spring and autumn conference dates.

### Is it cheaper to book a speaker directly or through a bureau?

Booking directly is often cheaper because there is no agency commission, which is typically 20% to 30% of the fee. A bureau saves you time on shortlisting, negotiation and contracts, so it can be worth the cost for large events or famous speakers.

### What should I look for when hiring a keynote speaker?

Look for a clear fit between the speaker's topics and your audience, real video of them speaking on stage, testimonials from event organizers, relevant past events and a professional one-sheet. A short call before booking helps you confirm they can tailor the talk.

### What is the difference between a keynote speaker and a motivational speaker?

A keynote speaker is defined by their role at the event: the featured talk that sets the theme. A motivational speaker is defined by their style and subject: inspiration and personal growth. Many motivational speakers deliver keynotes, but a keynote can also focus on leadership, technology, sales or industry trends.

### Can I hire a keynote speaker for a virtual event?

Yes. Many keynote speakers offer virtual keynotes, often at a lower fee because there is no travel. Ask for a recording of a previous virtual talk and confirm their camera, microphone and lighting setup before you book.

## Hire your next keynote speaker with confidence

Finding the right keynote speakers for hire comes down to a clear goal, a realistic budget and a simple vetting process. Start early, judge speakers on real video and organizer testimonials, and compare your finalists on the same criteria. The more consistent the information you start with, the faster the decision becomes.

Ready to start your shortlist? [Browse the Speakerfolio speaker directory](https://speakerfolio.com/speakers/) to compare speakers by topic and format, watch their talks and send a booking request directly.

# What Event Planners Look for on a Leadership Speaker's Website

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-event-planners-look-for-on-a-leadership-speaker-website/
Published: 2026-11-07 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

When event planners consider booking a leadership speaker, they need more than an impressive biography or professional photograph. They want evidence that the speaker fits their audience, delivers valuable presentations, and can work professionally with their event team. A well-organized leadership speaker website helps answer these questions and makes the booking decision easier.

Whether you are an experienced keynote speaker or building your speaking career, your website should work as a professional booking tool. It needs to communicate your expertise, demonstrate your presentation style, establish credibility, and provide a straightforward way for event organizers to contact you.

## 1. A Clear Leadership Speaking Position

The first thing event planners should understand is what you speak about and who benefits from your presentations. A headline such as "Leadership Speaker and Business Consultant" may describe your profession, but it does not explain your value. A stronger message identifies your audience, expertise, and the outcome your presentations help achieve.

For example, "Helping Business Leaders Build High-Performing Teams" communicates a specific focus. Your homepage should make this positioning visible without requiring visitors to explore several pages. Clear positioning also helps planners determine whether your expertise matches their conference theme, leadership program, or organizational objectives.

## 2. Specific Keynote Topics and Presentation Outcomes

Event planners need to understand what you can deliver before they consider your availability or speaking fee. List your keynote topics with descriptive titles, short explanations, and practical audience takeaways. Instead of presenting broad subjects such as leadership or motivation, explain the particular challenge each presentation addresses.

A leadership speaker might offer topics such as *Leading Through Organizational Change*, *Building High-Performance Teams*, and *Developing Future Leaders*. For each topic, explain who should attend, what the presentation covers, and what participants can learn. This helps organizers compare your sessions with their event objectives.

## 3. A Professional Speaker Biography

Your biography helps event planners understand your professional background and determine whether your experience supports your speaking message. Include relevant leadership positions, industry experience, achievements, publications, and qualifications. Prioritize information that demonstrates your expertise rather than listing every position you have held throughout your career.

Provide both a short and a longer biography when possible. A short version is useful for event agendas and promotional materials, while an extended version helps organizers introduce you to their audience. Your biography should also be easy to copy, download, or share with an event committee.

## 4. A Real Speaking Demo Video

A speaking video gives event planners a direct way to evaluate your communication style, stage presence, audience interaction, and presentation delivery. A professional headshot cannot demonstrate these qualities. Whenever possible, use genuine footage from a keynote, conference, workshop, or corporate presentation rather than relying entirely on a promotional montage.

Place your strongest video near the top of your website or on a clearly labeled speaking page. Choose footage that demonstrates your ability to communicate leadership ideas and engage an audience. Keep the video relevant to the type of event you want to attract, and ensure it plays properly on mobile devices.

## 5. Testimonials From Event Organizers

Testimonials reduce uncertainty because they provide evidence of how other organizations experienced working with you. Event planners often want to know whether a speaker delivered the promised presentation, understood the audience, followed the schedule, and contributed positively to the event.

Prioritize feedback from conference organizers, corporate clients, association leaders, and workshop coordinators. Include the person's name, professional role, organization, and event context when you have permission. Specific comments about presentation quality, audience engagement, and practical value are more informative than generic statements such as "Excellent speaker."

## 6. Previous Events and Speaking Experience

A dedicated speaking history section helps planners understand where you have presented and which audiences you have addressed. Include relevant conferences, corporate events, leadership summits, universities, professional associations, and workshops. When available, add event photographs, organization names, presentation titles, and dates to provide useful context.

Do not exaggerate your experience or display organization logos without permission. If you are an emerging speaker, include relevant webinars, panel discussions, workshops, and professional presentations instead. A transparent record of your experience is more valuable than an impressive-looking list that cannot be verified.

## 7. A Downloadable Speaker One-Sheet

A speaker one-sheet is a concise document that event planners can download, review, and share with colleagues or selection committees. It typically includes your photograph, professional biography, signature talks, speaking topics, key achievements, testimonials, and contact information. This saves organizers from collecting essential details manually across different website sections.

Make the document easy to download and suitable for professional sharing. Use a clear filename, readable typography, and consistent branding. If you have multiple presentation formats, mention them briefly so planners can understand whether you offer keynotes, workshops, panel participation, or virtual sessions.

## 8. Clear Speaking Formats and Technical Requirements

Not every event needs the same type of presentation. Some organizers require a short keynote, while others need an interactive workshop, executive session, panel discussion, or virtual presentation. Showing your available formats helps planners understand how your expertise can fit different event schedules and audience requirements.

Include typical presentation lengths and any important technical considerations. For example, mention whether you require a microphone, presentation screen, confidence monitor, or specific audio setup. You do not need to publish every technical detail on your homepage, but providing a clear starting point helps organizers plan more efficiently.

## 9. An Easy-to-Use Booking Enquiry Form

A website should make contacting you straightforward. Event planners should not have to search through social media profiles or guess which email address handles speaking enquiries. Place a visible booking button in the main navigation and include a dedicated contact section with a simple enquiry form.

A useful form can request the organizer's name, organization, email address, event date, location, audience size, preferred presentation topic, and event format. Avoid asking for unnecessary information before an initial conversation. Clearly explain what happens after submission and respond promptly so interested organizers can continue planning.

## 10. Professional Contact Information and Availability

Professional contact details reassure event planners that they can reach the right person when discussing an engagement. Use a dedicated business email address, a consistent professional identity, and links to relevant social profiles. If an assistant or booking representative manages enquiries, explain their role and provide the appropriate contact details.

You can also explain how organizers should enquire about availability, travel arrangements, and speaking fees. Publishing an exact fee is optional because pricing depends on event requirements and presentation formats. However, a clear enquiry process and timely communication help establish confidence before a booking agreement is discussed.

## 11. Mobile-Friendly Design and Fast Navigation

Many event planners discover speakers while researching conferences, reviewing recommendations, or comparing candidates between meetings. Your website should therefore work well on smartphones, tablets, and desktop computers. Important information such as your speaking topics, video, biography, and booking contact should remain easy to find on smaller screens.

Use readable typography, clear navigation, descriptive buttons, and appropriately sized images. Avoid unnecessary animations, oversized media files, and complicated menus that delay access to important information. A mobile-friendly website improves the visitor experience and supports search visibility, although design quality alone cannot guarantee higher rankings.

## 12. Search-Friendly Content That Demonstrates Expertise

Your website should explain your expertise using language that event planners and potential audiences naturally search for. Create dedicated sections for your leadership topics, presentation formats, professional background, and relevant industries. A page focused on leadership keynote speaking can provide more useful context than a homepage filled with generic promotional language.

Use descriptive page titles, meaningful headings, relevant internal links, and original content. Include location information if you serve particular regions, and describe virtual or international availability accurately. Google's guidance emphasizes helpful, original, people-first content rather than repetitive keyword placement, making useful speaker information a stronger foundation for long-term search visibility. [Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content).

## 13. Trust Signals and Consistent Professional Branding

A professional website should present a consistent identity across your biography, photographs, social profiles, presentation materials, and contact information. Use a recognizable headshot, consistent speaker name, professional email, and current information. These details help organizers confirm that they are reviewing the correct person and contacting an active professional.

Where relevant, include media appearances, published articles, books, professional memberships, awards, and industry affiliations. Only display credentials and endorsements that you can substantiate. Trust comes from accurate information and relevant evidence, not from adding as many badges or logos as possible.

## Why Speakerfolio Is a Practical Starting Point for Leadership Speakers

Building a professional speaker website from scratch can involve design, development, hosting, content preparation, and ongoing maintenance. Independent speakers may not need to manage all these tasks before they have established a consistent booking pipeline. A dedicated speaker platform can provide a more focused starting point for presenting their expertise online.

[Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/) is designed for keynote speakers, trainers, and coaches who want a professional website and greater discoverability. Speakers can get a designed website, choose from six templates, and receive a directory listing. Their profiles can present speaking topics, stage videos, past events, and booking enquiries, helping event planners evaluate potential speakers.

Speakerfolio also supports direct booking enquiries, so organizers can contact speakers without a platform booking fee. Premium options include custom design, a personal domain, and hosting. For leadership speakers who want to establish an online presence without starting with a fully custom website project, Speakerfolio provides a practical way to bring important speaker information together.

## A Leadership Speaker Website Checklist for Event Planners

Before publishing your website, review it from an event organizer's perspective. Can someone understand your expertise, evaluate your presentation, and contact you without unnecessary effort? The following checklist covers the essential information that should be available on a professional leadership speaker website.

- Clear leadership speaking headline and positioning
- Specific keynote topics with audience outcomes
- Professional biography in short and long formats
- Recent speaking demo video
- Testimonials from relevant clients and organizers
- Previous events and speaking experience
- Downloadable speaker one-sheet
- Available presentation formats and durations
- Simple booking enquiry form
- Professional contact information
- Mobile-friendly design and clear navigation
- Relevant, original content for search visibility

A website does not need dozens of pages to be effective. It needs to answer the questions that matter to the people making the booking decision. Prioritize the information that demonstrates relevance, credibility, presentation quality, and professional communication.

## Frequently asked questions

### What do event planners look for on a leadership speaker's website?

Event planners generally look for relevant speaking topics, a professional biography, presentation videos, testimonials, previous event experience, and clear contact information. They also need to understand how your presentation fits their audience, event format, and budget. A strong website makes this information easy to evaluate and share.

### Does a leadership speaker need a personal website?

A personal website gives leadership speakers a central place to present their expertise, speaking topics, videos, testimonials, and booking information. It also provides a destination that can be shared through LinkedIn, email proposals, conference applications, and professional referrals. A dedicated speaker platform such as Speakerfolio can help simplify the process of creating one.

### Should speakers display their fees on their websites?

Displaying speaking fees is optional. Some speakers publish starting rates or presentation packages, while others prefer to discuss pricing after learning about the event. If fees vary by presentation length, audience, location, travel, and preparation requirements, a booking enquiry form can help collect the information needed for an accurate proposal.

### How long should a speaker demo video be?

A short, focused demo is generally easier for event planners to review than a long recording. A video of approximately two to three minutes can highlight presentation delivery, audience interaction, and relevant speaking experience. The most important factor is showing authentic, high-quality footage that demonstrates what organizers can expect.

### How can a new leadership speaker build credibility without major event experience?

New speakers can demonstrate expertise through professional workshops, webinars, panel discussions, internal corporate presentations, and relevant industry contributions. They should collect genuine feedback, record suitable presentation footage, and publish clear information about their experience. Honest evidence of relevant expertise is more effective than presenting an inflated speaking history.

### What is the best platform for building a leadership speaker website?

The best platform depends on the speaker's needs, budget, technical experience, and desired level of customization. General website builders provide broad design flexibility, while dedicated speaker platforms focus on speaker profiles and booking information. [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/) offers a speaker-focused option with a designed website, directory listing, and booking enquiries.

## Final Thoughts

An effective leadership speaker website is more than an online biography. It is a decision-making resource that helps event planners understand your expertise, evaluate your presentation, verify your credibility, and contact you about an engagement. The strongest websites make these steps clear without overwhelming visitors with unnecessary information.

Start with the essentials: specific leadership topics, a professional biography, genuine speaking footage, relevant testimonials, and a straightforward booking process. Then improve your website as your speaking career develops. With a focused online presence and a platform such as Speakerfolio, you can make it easier for event planners to discover, evaluate, and enquire about booking you.

# Free vs Paid Keynote Speaker Websites: What You Actually Need

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/free-vs-paid-keynote-speaker-websites/
Published: 2026-11-05 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

Most keynote speakers do not need an expensive website to get booked. They need a fast, professional page that shows their talks, a stage video, proof from past events and a clear way to book. A free speaker website covers that well, and a paid website makes sense once you want your own domain and more pages.

This guide compares free and paid keynote speaker websites side by side. You will see what each option includes, where free website builders hold you back, and the point at which paying for a website starts to earn you more bookings. It ends with a simple rule you can use to decide today.

## The short answer

Start with a free speaker website if you are new to speaking, have up to four talks or need a credible link to send planners this week. Upgrade to a paid website when you have a strong brand, steady bookings and want your own domain. The right choice depends on your stage, not on the price.

Either way, the content matters more than the platform. Planners judge your topic, your video and your proof first, then your design. A clean free site with a clear booking path will outperform an expensive site that hides your talks three clicks deep.

## What a free keynote speaker website gives you

A good free speaker website gives you one well-organised page with your bio, talks, stage video, testimonials and a booking form. It loads on a phone, it looks professional, and it costs nothing to keep online. For a speaker who has nothing yet, it is a big step up from a LinkedIn profile.

The trade-off is control. You usually get a subdomain such as yourname.speakerfolio.com rather than yourname.com, fewer pages, and a small credit in the footer. Many general website builders also add their own branding or ads to free sites, which is the main thing to check before you sign up.

## The hidden costs of free website builders

General builders are free to start but rarely free to finish. Wix, for example, says its free sites use a wixsite.com address and show Wix branding, and sometimes ads. Removing ads and connecting a custom domain starts with its paid Light plan, which Wix lists at $17 per month billed annually.

The bigger cost is your time. A blank builder expects you to write the copy, choose a layout, add a booking form and make it work on mobile yourself. Many speakers spend weeks on a site that still misses what planners look for, which is why a speaker-specific service is often the better free option.

## What a paid keynote speaker website adds

A paid website gives you your own domain, a custom design and as many pages as you need. You can add a page for each talk, a media kit, a blog and booking details for different event types. You also remove any platform credit, so every visitor sees only your brand.

Paid also means more ways to be found. Separate talk pages and articles can rank in Google for searches such as "resilience speaker for healthcare", and full SEO and AI visibility setup helps tools like ChatGPT describe you correctly. These gains matter most once you already have proof and a clear speaking topic.

## Free vs paid speaker websites compared

| Feature | Free speaker website | Paid speaker website |
|---|---|---|
| Web address | yourname.speakerfolio.com | yourname.com |
| Design | Professional template | Custom design for your brand |
| Pages | One page | As many as you need |
| Talks, video, testimonials, booking form | Included | Included |
| Footer credit or builder ads | Small credit on Speakerfolio; ads on some builders | None |
| SEO and AI visibility | Basic setup | Full setup |
| Best for | New and growing speakers | Established speakers and brands |

The table shows that the core booking tools are the same on both plans. What you pay for is your own address, more pages, full control of your brand and deeper search setup. If you do not need those yet, paying early adds cost without adding bookings.

## Why your web address matters to event planners

Trust drives bookings, and your address is part of that first impression. Stanford's Web Credibility guidelines advise sites to show that real, trustworthy people stand behind them, make contact easy, look professional and use restraint with promotional content such as ads. A cluttered free site with builder ads breaks several of those rules at once.

A clean subdomain from a speaker platform does not hurt you when the page itself is professional and ad-free. A custom domain becomes more valuable as you grow, because it appears on your one-sheet, slides and email signature. It also stays yours if you ever change platforms, so your links never break.

## Speed and first impressions decide the booking

Planners give your page seconds, not minutes. Research by Jakob Nielsen at Nielsen Norman Group found that users often leave web pages within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a page must communicate its value proposition within about 10 seconds. Your topic and video need to be visible straight away.

Load time matters just as much on a phone. Google's study The Need for Mobile Speed found that 53% of mobile site visits are abandoned if pages take longer than three seconds to load. Whether your site is free or paid, choose a platform that keeps pages fast and light.

## When a free speaker website is enough

A free website is enough when you are building your speaking business, testing a new topic or need a professional link quickly. It works well if you have one to four talks, a short demo reel and a few testimonials. Most new speakers get more value from finishing their content than from paying for design.

It is also the smart choice when your budget is better spent elsewhere. A professional headshot, a two-minute demo reel or a few showcase events will usually win you more bookings than a custom design. You can always move up to a paid site once the bookings justify it.

## When it is time to pay for a speaker website

Upgrade when your speaking business is clearly growing. Signs include regular paid bookings, a book or signature program, media coverage, several distinct talks or bureau interest. At that stage, your own domain and a custom design make you look like the established expert you already are.

Pay when you need features a one-page site cannot hold. That includes separate talk pages for search, a media kit, a speaker blog or several audiences such as corporate events and schools. If you find yourself cutting content to fit one page, it is time for more room.

## How Speakerfolio handles free and paid websites

Speakerfolio was built for speakers, so the free plan already includes what planners look for. You get a one-page portfolio on yourname.speakerfolio.com, six professional templates, your talks, stage video, testimonials, a booking form and a speaker one-sheet. We write and set it up from your LinkedIn profile, with no ads and no card.

Premium moves you to your own domain with a custom design, as many pages as you need, full admin access and no Speakerfolio credit. Hosting with SSL and backups is included, and you can add 20 branded social media posts a month. Every Speakerfolio speaker can also be listed in the directory where planners search.

## How to choose the right website builder

If you are weighing Speakerfolio against Wix, Squarespace, WordPress and other tools, compare them on the features planners need rather than on templates alone. Check booking forms, video embeds, mobile speed and the real cost once ads and branding are removed. A side-by-side review saves you from switching later.

We compared the most popular options in [Best Website Builders for Motivational Speakers Compared: Free and Paid](https://medium.com/@imsaleh/best-website-builders-for-motivational-speakers-compared-free-and-paid-98d71a7453b2). It covers pricing, ease of use and which builders suit new versus established speakers. Read it alongside this guide before you commit to a paid plan anywhere.

## Your bio matters more than your plan

Free or paid, your speaker bio is the text planners read, copy and paste into their programmes. A strong bio states who you help, the result you deliver and the proof behind it, in a length that fits an event page. Without it, even the best design will not get you shortlisted.

Our guide [How to Write a Motivational Speaker Bio That Gets You Booked](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-write-motivational-speaker-bio-gets-you-booked-speakerfolio-s8zvc/) walks you through a simple formula with examples. Use it to write your one-line, short and long bio before you build anything. For a full list of what belongs on your site, read the [motivational speaker website checklist](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/motivational-speaker-website-checklist/) and [what every speaker website needs](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-every-speaker-website-needs/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a free website good enough for a keynote speaker?

Yes, if it is professional, fast and ad-free. Planners care most about your topic, video, testimonials and an easy way to book. A free speaker website that shows those clearly is enough for new and growing speakers, and you can upgrade to your own domain later without starting again.

### How much does a keynote speaker website cost?

A speaker website can cost nothing on a free plan, around $100 to $300 a year on a builder or managed plan, or several thousand dollars for a custom agency build. Speakerfolio's free plan costs nothing. Premium is $100 a year, currently $80 with the Black Friday offer, including hosting.

### Do I need my own domain as a speaker?

You do not need one to start, but it helps as you grow. A domain such as yourname.com looks established, fits neatly on slides and business cards, and stays yours if you change platforms. Most domains cost $10 to $20 a year from a registrar.

### Do free website builders show ads?

Some do. Wix, for example, says its free sites show Wix branding and sometimes ads, and use a wixsite.com address. Speakerfolio's free speaker websites show no ads, only a small designer credit in the footer, which you can remove by upgrading to Premium.

### Can I move from a free website to a paid one later?

Yes. On Speakerfolio you keep your content, and Premium moves your site to your own domain with a custom design and old links redirected. That means you can start free today, build your proof, and upgrade only when your bookings make the extra cost worthwhile.

## The verdict: start free, upgrade with your bookings

For most keynote speakers, the smartest path is to launch a free, professional website now and upgrade when your speaking business demands it. Spend your early budget on video and proof, not on design. A clear site that planners can trust will win you more bookings than an expensive one.

Speakerfolio gives you a free speaker website, written and built for you from your LinkedIn profile, live in about two days. You see a private preview before anything goes live. [Get your free speaker website](https://speakerfolio.com/contact/#start), or compare plans on our [pricing page](https://speakerfolio.com/pricing/) when you are ready for your own domain.

# What Should a Motivational Speaker Website Include? A Planner's Checklist

URL: https://speakerfolio.com/articles/motivational-speaker-website-checklist/
Published: 2026-11-01 · Author: Saleh, Speakerfolio

An event planner has a shortlist of five speakers and an afternoon to decide. They open five browser tabs. Within a few minutes, two of those tabs are closed.

They didn't close them because the speakers were bad. They closed them because the websites didn't answer the planner's questions fast enough. Where's the video? What does this person actually talk about? Have they spoken to an audience like mine? How do I check if they're free on 14 May?

This guide looks at your **motivational speaker website** from the other side of the screen. It's built around the questions planners, meeting organizers and speaker bureaus ask when they review a speaker, and it turns those questions into a checklist you can work through section by section.

If you're building your site from scratch, [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/) builds a one-page speaker website for you, free, with these sections already in place. If you already have a site, use the checklist as an audit.

## How event planners actually review a speaker website

Before the checklist, it helps to know what a planner is doing when they land on your site. In most cases, they're not browsing. They're trying to rule you in or out quickly, and then defend their choice to someone else: a boss, a committee or a client.

That gives a planner four jobs:

1. **Check fit.** Does this speaker talk about the theme of our event, for an audience like ours?
2. **Check quality.** Are they actually good on stage? Will the audience stay in their seats?
3. **Check risk.** Have other organizers booked them and been happy? Will they be easy to work with?
4. **Check logistics.** Are they available, roughly in budget, and easy to contact?

Every item in the checklist below serves one of those four jobs. If something on your site doesn't help a planner check fit, quality, risk or logistics, it's probably clutter.

**Tip:** Planners often share your link with people who never met you. Write every page so it makes sense to someone forwarded the URL with no context.

## The motivational speaker website checklist at a glance

Here is the full list. Each item is explained in the sections that follow.

| # | What to include | Planner's question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A clear headline above the fold | "Who is this and what do they talk about?" |
| 2 | Demo reel or full-length video | "Are they good on stage?" |
| 3 | Signature keynote topics | "Do they fit our theme?" |
| 4 | Audience outcomes | "What will our people take away?" |
| 5 | Short and long speaker bios | "What's their story, and can I copy it?" |
| 6 | Testimonials from event organizers | "Did other planners like them?" |
| 7 | Client logos and past events | "Have they spoken to people like ours?" |
| 8 | Downloadable one-sheet and media kit | "Can I send this to my committee?" |
| 9 | Professional photos and headshots | "Can I use these in our promotion?" |
| 10 | Books, podcast or media appearances | "Are they credible beyond the stage?" |
| 11 | Speaking formats and delivery options | "Can they do a workshop, virtual session or emcee?" |
| 12 | Simple booking or inquiry form | "How do I check availability?" |
| 13 | Fee guidance or a clear next step | "Is this in our budget?" |
| 14 | Upcoming and past engagements | "Are they active and in demand?" |
| 15 | Mobile speed and easy navigation | "Can I review this on my phone between meetings?" |
| 16 | Search and AI visibility basics | "Can I find them when I search for a topic?" |

## Section 1: First impressions (fit at a glance)

### 1. A clear headline above the fold

The top of your home page has one job: tell a planner who you are, what you speak about, and who you speak to. Most speaker sites waste it on a big photo and a vague line like "Inspiring audiences worldwide."

A stronger headline names your topic and audience:

- **Weak:** "Igniting passion. Unlocking potential."
- **Stronger:** "Keynotes on resilience and change for healthcare and frontline teams."

Under the headline, add one short sentence on what makes you different (your story, your method or your results) and two buttons: **Watch my reel** and **Check availability**.

**Tip:** Read your headline out loud and ask, "Could a planner tell my topic without scrolling?" If the answer is no, rewrite it.

### 2. A demo reel and at least one full-length talk

Video is the closest a planner gets to seeing you live. It's usually the first thing they look for, and the main way they judge quality.

Include two types of video:

- **A demo reel (2 to 4 minutes):** your best moments, real audience reactions, and a clear sense of your energy and humor. Put this near the top of your home page.
- **A longer clip (10 minutes or more):** an uncut section of a real talk. Experienced planners want to see that you can hold a room, not just that you have good highlights.

Keep video recent, show real audiences (wide shots of a full room help), and make sure it plays well on a phone. Avoid autoplaying with sound. No reel yet? Our guide to [making a two-minute speaker reel from footage you already have](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/make-a-two-minute-speaker-reel-from-footage-you-already-have/) walks you through it.

Every Speakerfolio template has a stage video section, so your reel sits on the page where planners look for it.

### 3. Signature keynote topics

Planners book topics, not people in general. Give each of your signature talks its own block, or its own page if you have several.

For each topic, include:

- **A specific title** that a planner could put straight into a conference agenda.
- **A two- or three-sentence description** of the problem the talk addresses.
- **Who it's for:** industries, roles or event types it works best with.
- **Formats available:** keynote, breakout, workshop, virtual.

Keep it to three to five topics. A list of twelve makes you look like a generalist, and a planner hunting for a resilience speaker will trust the person who focuses on resilience.

### 4. Audience outcomes

A motivational talk can sound fluffy to a buyer who needs to justify the spend. Make the result concrete. Under each topic, list three things the audience will leave with.

**Example:** "After this keynote, your team will:

- Have a simple three-step reset they can use under pressure.
- Know how to talk about setbacks without blame.
- Leave with a 30-day challenge they can start the next morning."

Outcomes help planners sell you internally. They can paste them straight into an event brief.

## Section 2: Proof and credibility (quality and risk)

### 5. Short and long speaker bios

Planners need your bio for programs, introductions, event apps and press releases. Make it easy to copy.

Provide three lengths:

- **One line (about 25 words)** for agendas and social posts.
- **Short bio (about 100 words)** for event programs.
- **Long bio (250 to 400 words)** for the website and media.

Write all three in the third person, lead with what you speak about rather than your childhood, and include the one story or credential that makes you worth hearing. Add a separate **introduction script** the emcee can read on the day; planners appreciate it more than you'd expect. For a step-by-step version, read [how to write a speaker bio planners can actually use](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/how-to-write-a-speaker-bio-planners-can-actually-use/).

### 6. Testimonials from event organizers

Audience praise is nice. Praise from someone who booked you is what a planner trusts, because that person had the same job they do.

Strong testimonials include:

- **The person's name, role and organization**, not "Sarah, HR."
- **The event type and audience size**, if possible.
- **A specific result:** "highest-rated session of the conference," "our team still uses her three-step reset."
- **A comment on working with you:** easy to work with, customized the talk, arrived early for tech checks.

Place two or three testimonials on your home page and the rest on each topic page, matched to the talk they're about. A short video testimonial from an organizer is even better. Here's [how to ask for testimonials right after the event](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/ask-for-testimonials-the-right-way-right-after-the-event/), when organizers are happiest to give them.

### 7. Client logos and past events

Logos answer "Have they spoken to people like us?" in a glance. Show organizations you've spoken for, grouped by industry if you serve several (for example, healthcare, education, sales teams).

Only use logos you have permission to display, and keep the list honest. A planner who calls a reference and finds you spoke at a breakfast meeting, not the annual conference, will quietly drop you.

### 8. A downloadable one-sheet and media kit

A **speaker one-sheet** is a single page (usually a PDF) that summarizes you: photo, headline, topics, short bio, a few testimonials, logos and contact details. Planners use it to pitch you to their committee.

Your media kit can add:

- Headshots and action photos (see item 9)
- All three bio lengths and your introduction script
- Topic descriptions and outcomes
- Technical and room requirements (your **speaker rider**)
- Logos and testimonials

Put a visible **Download one-sheet** button on your home page and booking page. Don't hide it behind an email form; planners in a hurry will skip it.

A free speaker one-sheet comes with every Speakerfolio site, ready to send to planners.

### 9. Professional photos and headshots

Planners need images for brochures, event websites and social posts. Provide:

- **A recent headshot** in color, in both portrait and landscape crops.
- **Action shots** of you on stage with an audience visible.
- **High-resolution downloads** with clear usage permission.

Label the files with your name (for example, `jane-doe-headshot.jpg`), so they don't get lost in a planner's downloads folder.

### 10. Books, podcasts and media appearances

If you've written a book, host a podcast or appeared in the press, add a short **As featured in** section. Third-party mentions do two things: they show credibility beyond the stage, and they give planners extra material (a book bundle for attendees, a podcast episode to share before the event).

Link each mention to the source so the claim is easy to check.

## Section 3: Logistics and booking (make it easy to say yes)

### 11. Speaking formats and delivery options

Many events need more than a 45-minute keynote. Spell out what you offer:

- Keynote (in-person)
- Breakout or workshop session
- Half-day or full-day training
- Virtual or hybrid keynote
- Emcee or host
- Fireside chat or panel moderator

For virtual talks, mention your setup in a sentence (studio, camera, lighting, backup internet). It removes a common worry.

### 12. A simple booking or inquiry form

This is where many speaker websites lose bookings. The form is buried in the footer, asks fifteen questions, or is just an email address.

Make your booking page easy to find (in the top menu, labeled **Book [Your Name]** or **Check availability**) and keep the form short. Ask for:

- Name, organization and email
- Event date and location (or "virtual")
- Event type and audience size
- Topic of interest
- Budget range (optional, as a dropdown)
- Anything else they want you to know

Then tell them what happens next: "I'll reply within one business day with availability and a short call link." That single sentence reduces uncertainty and makes planners more likely to send the form.

Every Speakerfolio site includes a booking form, so inquiries come straight to you.

### 13. Fee guidance or a clear next step

Speakers often avoid listing fees, and that's fine. But a planner with a fixed budget doesn't want to spend a call finding out you're out of range.

Pick one approach:

- **Show a range:** "Keynote fees start at $7,500 plus travel."
- **Show tiers:** virtual, regional and international.
- **Explain how pricing works** ("fees depend on format, location and date") and offer a quick call.

Any of these is better than silence. If you work with a speaker bureau, say so and explain whether planners should contact you or your agent.

### 14. Upcoming and past engagements

A short **Upcoming events** list shows you're active and in demand. A **Past engagements** list shows range and experience.

Keep it current. A calendar where the last event is from three years ago does more harm than having no calendar at all.

## Section 4: Technical basics (don't lose them on the way in)

### 15. Mobile speed and easy navigation

Many planners review speakers between meetings on a phone. Check your site on your own phone and ask:

- Does the home page load quickly?
- Does the reel play without zooming or rotating?
- Can you reach the booking form in two taps?
- Is the text readable without pinching?

Keep your main menu short: **About, Topics, Video, Testimonials, Book**. Anything else can live in the footer.

### 16. Search and AI visibility basics

Planners don't only arrive from your business card. Many start with a search like "resilience keynote speaker for nurses" or ask an AI assistant for speaker suggestions. Help them find you:

- **Use your topic words** in page titles and headings, not just your name.
- **Give each signature talk its own page** with a clear title and description.
- **Write a plain-language FAQ** answering the questions planners ask (formats, travel, customization).
- **Keep your name, topics and bio consistent** across your website, LinkedIn, speaker directories and bureau listings, so search engines and AI tools see the same story everywhere.
- **Add alt text** to photos describing what's in them.

Speakerfolio sites come with a basic AI visibility setup, so search engines and AI assistants can read your topics and bio.

## Common mistakes on motivational speaker websites

Even good speakers lose bookings to these:

- **All about you, nothing about the audience.** Your story matters, but planners buy outcomes for their people.
- **No video, or only a five-year-old clip.** Planners will assume your current talks aren't as strong.
- **Testimonials with no names.** "Amazing speaker! - J." doesn't reduce anyone's risk.
- **Booking hidden in the footer.** If a planner can't find the next step, they move to the next tab.
- **Too many topics.** Five focused talks beat twelve vague ones.
- **Out-of-date content.** Old photos, past events from years ago or broken links make you look inactive.

For a shorter version of this list, see [what every speaker website needs](https://speakerfolio.com/articles/what-every-speaker-website-needs/).

You can build a speaker site on any general website builder, but you'll spend time working out the structure yourself. [Speakerfolio](https://speakerfolio.com/) is built only for speakers, trainers and coaches, so the sections planners look for are there from the start:

- **Six speaker templates** to choose from. [See the templates](https://speakerfolio.com/templates/).

## Frequently asked questions

### What should a motivational speaker website include?

At minimum: a clear headline naming your topic and audience, a demo reel, your signature keynote topics with audience outcomes, testimonials from event organizers, client logos, a downloadable one-sheet, professional photos, and a simple booking form. Fee guidance, an events calendar and media mentions make it stronger.

### What do event planners look for on a speaker website?

Planners look for four things: fit (does your topic match their event and audience), quality (usually judged from video), risk (testimonials and past clients) and logistics (formats, availability, budget and how to contact you). A site that answers all four quickly gets more inquiries.

### How long should a speaker demo reel be?

Most demo reels run two to four minutes. Pair it with a longer, uncut clip of 10 minutes or more so planners can see you hold a room, not just your best highlights.

### Should I put my speaking fee on my website?

You don't have to list an exact fee, but give planners some guidance, such as a starting range or an explanation of what affects price. It saves both sides time and filters out events that can't afford you.

### What is a speaker one-sheet?

A speaker one-sheet is a one-page summary, usually a PDF, that includes your photo, topics, short bio, testimonials, client logos and contact details. Planners use it to pitch you to a committee or decision-maker.

### Do I need a separate website if I'm listed with a speaker bureau?

Yes. A bureau listing helps, but your own website is where you control your story, video, topics and booking path. Many planners check a speaker's own site even when they found them through a bureau.

## Turn your website into your best booking tool

A motivational speaker website isn't a digital brochure. It's the place a planner decides whether to take the next step. Go through the checklist, fix the gaps that stop a planner checking fit, quality, risk and logistics, and keep your video, testimonials and calendar fresh.
